real-time-systems-q1.testing: whether you answer with a chain of stages and owners, not one number.
real-time-systems-q1.spoken:
Beat Say
1 · The human number "Humans leave gaps of roughly 200 to 300 milliseconds between turns. Past about 800 a pause reads as lag, and past a second and a half people start talking over it. So I'd set a target like 800 milliseconds at p95 from the moment the user stops to the first sound back."
2 · Budget is a chain "And I treat it as a chain, not a number: deciding the user has finished, getting the final transcript to the logic, deciding what to say, the model's first token if a model generates it, the first audio byte from TTS, and the network and jitter buffer back. Every hop adds."
3 · Where it goes "In our design budget that is 150 to 250 for turn detection, about 20 milliseconds of our own logic, 300 for TTS first byte, and 60 to 120 of network: about 530 typical and 690 at p95."
4 · The two levers "Two slices dominate. Endpointing, how long you wait to be sure they have finished, is a choice and not a constant. And generation plus synthesis."
5 · How we set ours "In our interview platform the target is 450 at p50 and 800 at p95, and no model generation is in the budget: that happens while the candidate is still talking."
Close "A sub-second chain, with endpointing and generation as the two levers."

real-time-systems-q2.testing: that you optimise time to first audio, not total response time, and that you measure it at the right percentile.
real-time-systems-q2.trap: optimising end-to-end completion time while the first sound is still slow.
real-time-systems-q2.spoken:
Beat Say
1 · Plain definition "The user feels time to first audio: the silence between when they stop talking and when they hear the first sound back."
2 · Why first audio, not completion "They hear the start of a reply, not the end, so total generation time barely matters as long as audio keeps flowing once it starts."
3 · How to shape it "That is why everything streams. The first TTS chunk plays while the model is still generating, and TTS starts on the first sentence. In our system we split the text at sentence ends or every 12 words, with a TTS stream per segment, which took first audio on a long unpunctuated sentence from 677 to 437 milliseconds. Perceived latency can also be shaped: a short, honest bridge line buys about a second and a half without dead air. What we don't do is fake it with synthesised ums."
4 · What to measure "I measure p95 of first audio per turn, not average end-to-end per session."
5 · Where it bites "It bites on the first turn, with cold connections, and in the tail, when a vendor queues under load."
Close "Optimise the first sound, keep audio flowing, and measure it per turn at p95."

real-time-systems-q3.testing: whether you know which work can move before the endpoint, and that every overlap trades wasted compute for latency.
real-time-systems-q3.trap: a strict STT → LLM → TTS chain, then blaming the models for being slow.
real-time-systems-q3.spoken:
Beat Say
1 · The one-line claim "The principle: anything that can happen while the user is still talking shouldn't be on the clock after they stop."
2 · Work during speech "Streaming STT gives interim transcripts every few hundred milliseconds, and work can start on those. In our system each final phrase triggers the analysis agents, scoring, gap-finding and integrity, debounced and restarted as the answer grows, so an insight is usually ready at the endpoint."
3 · Speculate on partials "The design goes further with speculative pre-generation: draft two to four candidate next questions during speech, fully rendered, and at the endpoint just pick one in about 10 milliseconds. The prototype uses LiveKit's preemptive generation, a cheaper version: start the reply before the end of turn is confirmed and throw it away if they keep talking."
4 · Stream into TTS "Then overlap generation with synthesis: chunk the text at sentence boundaries, or every 12 words, and start a TTS stream per chunk, so the first sentence plays while the rest is generated."
5 · Keep everything warm "And keep everything warm: connections to STT and TTS open before the first word, models loaded before the job arrives. A cold TLS connect to our TTS vendor from India was about 620 milliseconds."
6 · What it costs "Every overlap spends compute that gets discarded. Speculation is two to three times the tokens."
Close "That is the price of feeling like one fast interviewer."

stages.name: Stream into TTS
stages.html:
Prove it — how the chunker splits a long question (run with Python 3):

import re
END = re.compile(r"[.!?…]['\")\]]*$")
def segments(words, max_words=12):
    seg = []
    for w in words:
        seg.append(w)
        if END.search(w) or len(seg) >= max_words:
            yield " ".join(seg); seg = []
    if seg: yield " ".join(seg)
text = ("Walk me through how you would shard the ledger table when one tenant "
        "writes ten times more than the rest and reads must stay consistent. Take your time.")
for s in segments(text.split()): print(len(s.split()), "|", s)
# → 12 | Walk me through how you would shard the ledger table when one
# → 12 | tenant writes ten times more than the rest and reads must stay
# → 1 | consistent.
# → 3 | Take your time.

The first 12 words go to TTS without waiting for the full stop. The one-word tail is the cost of a forced flush.

real-time-systems-q4.testing: whether you separate true physical limits from things that only look fixed, and whether region placement is on your list.
real-time-systems-q4.trap: treating model load or cold connections as part of the floor.
real-time-systems-q4.spoken:
Beat Say
1 · Plain definition "The true floor is physics plus framing: what no engineering removes."
2 · Physics: distance "Light in fibre covers roughly 200 kilometres per millisecond, and real routes are longer than straight lines, so an intercontinental round trip is tens to a couple of hundred milliseconds. That makes region placement a latency decision: media, inference and TTS should sit near the user. In our design, for an Indian product, regional against distant is roughly 15 against 90 milliseconds, which is 13 percent of the turn budget spent before any work."
3 · Framing and buffering "Then audio framing: frames are 10 to 20 milliseconds, and the jitter buffer on the listener's side holds a few frames. Together with the network that is 60 to 120 milliseconds in our budget."
4 · The avoidable "floor" "What people call a floor but isn't: model load time, cold TLS handshakes, scaling from zero. Those are avoidable with warm pools. Our cold connect to the TTS vendor from India was about 620 milliseconds, on the first turn only."
5 · Where we placed things "So we placed the media server and agents in one Indian region."
Close "State the floor out loud, then show what you optimise above it."

real-time-systems-q5.testing: the stages in order, the control loops running beside them, and where state lives.
real-time-systems-q5.trap: describing a request/response API. The state and the interruption loop are the hard parts.
real-time-systems-q5.spoken:
Beat Say
1 · It's a session, not a request "First framing: this is a long-lived, stateful session, not a request and response service. Every stage streams, and every stage has its own timeout and fallback."
2 · The audio path, in order "In order: the browser captures the mic with echo cancellation, noise suppression and gain control. Audio goes as Opus over WebRTC to a LiveKit SFU, which forwards it without transcoding to the agent's job process. There Krisp cleans the input, Silero VAD says whether there is speech, Deepgram streaming STT produces interim and final transcripts with keyterms, and LiveKit's turn-detection model decides whether the candidate has finished. When the turn commits, rules pick the move, a speaker agent phrases it, and the text goes to TTS in sentence-sized chunks, back through the SFU."
3 · The two control loops "Two control loops run beside it. Barge-in: if the candidate speaks while the agent is talking, the agent stops within about half a second and the record keeps only what was heard. And turn state: who holds the floor, what was delivered, where the plan is."
4 · Who owns what "LiveKit owns audio, VAD, turn detection and interruption mechanics. We own everything where an audio event has a scoring consequence: echo, vocabulary, truncation bookkeeping, degradation."
5 · Per-turn observability "And everything is observed per turn: end-of-turn delay, STT delay, model first token, TTS first byte, end to end."
Close "A session with a streaming audio path, two control loops beside it, and numbers per turn."

real-time-systems-q6.testing: that you separate VAD, endpointing and turn detection, and treat the threshold as the biggest tunable slice of the budget.
real-time-systems-q6.spoken:
Beat Say
1 · Three different questions "It is three questions, not one. VAD asks whether there is speech in this 30-millisecond frame. Endpointing asks whether this utterance has ended. Turn detection asks whether the person has finished their turn, or is pausing to think."
2 · Why a silence timer fails "A fixed silence threshold forces a bad trade: 150 milliseconds interrupts anyone who pauses mid-thought, and 500 still cuts some people off and makes the agent feel slow."
3 · How a semantic model decides "So the better approach is semantic: a model that reads the last few turns of text alongside the audio. I'd shard by tenant, full stop, is complete; I used Kubernetes for the, is not, even after the same pause. We use LiveKit's end-of-turn model for that, with Silero VAD underneath and the STT vendor's own endpointing switched off, so there is one authority."
4 · Tuning it "The settings are a minimum wait of 0.8 seconds when the turn sounds finished and up to 3.5 seconds when the model thinks they are mid-thought. We started at 0.5 and it cut answers at thinking pauses."
5 · Where it breaks "It breaks on noise and accents. Noise can make VAD see speech that isn't there, and the turn model is English-only by its vendor's statement, so cut-off rates need measuring per accent."
Close "Cutting off a thinker is a fairness problem in an interview, not just UX."

real-time-systems-q7.testing: the full mechanism — detection, cancellation of audio and generation, history reconciliation, false positives — not just "we stop talking".
real-time-systems-q7.trap: logging the full generated reply into history when the user heard four words of it.
real-time-systems-q7.spoken:
Beat Say
1 · The one-line claim "That is barge-in, and the agent should yield immediately. Finishing the sentence reads as rude and robotic."
2 · Detect on sound "Detection has to be acoustic. Voice activity detection fires on the user's voice within a few hundred milliseconds; the transcript would arrive 200 to 300 later, by which point the agent has spoken over them. In our system it is LiveKit's VAD mode: 0.4 seconds of voice while the agent is speaking."
3 · Stop everything upstream "Then stop everything upstream, not just the speaker: stop consuming the TTS stream, flush the audio already queued for sending, and cancel the model generation, or you pay for tokens nobody hears."
4 · Record what was heard "Then reconcile state. The history must record what the user actually heard, truncated and marked interrupted, not what was generated. In an interview product, a question they only half-heard can't count as asked."
5 · Not every sound is a turn "Not every sound is an interruption. We ignore voice under 0.4 seconds, and if no words arrive within two seconds the agent resumes where it stopped. And echo has to be cancelled first, or the agent barges in on itself."
6 · So what for the system "So I track barge-ins by source, and the false-positive rate."
Close "Yield on sound, stop the whole pipeline, and store what was heard."

real-time-systems-q8.spoken:

1 · What each one is "Streaming STT emits interim transcripts every few hundred milliseconds: fast, but revisable. The model can change earlier words as more audio arrives. Then it emits a final for a phrase, which is stable."
2 · Partials for responsiveness "Partials are for responsiveness: live captions, early intent, and speculative work that can be thrown away."
3 · Finals for commitment "Finals are for commitment. Anything with a side effect, a tool call, a record, a transfer, waits for the final. A decision you would regret if the words changed must not be made on a partial."
4 · Confidence gates action "Confidence gates action: low confidence on something high-stakes means confirm, not act."
5 · How we use them "In our system Deepgram sends interims about every 300 milliseconds; they drive the captions and LiveKit's preemptive generation, which is discardable. The analysis agents trigger on final phrases, debounced 300 milliseconds. The candidate's turn is committed only when the turn detector says they are done, and only then is it written to the transcript and used by Chair. STT confidence is used only to ask for a repeat and never reaches the scorer, for fairness."
Close "Draft on partials, commit on finals."

1 · The one-line claim "Stream at sentence granularity: sentence-sized, bounded, and pipelined."
2 · Chunk on boundaries "Synthesis needs a complete phrase for natural intonation, so chunk on sentence or clause boundaries. But bound the worst case, because models sometimes produce a long sentence with no punctuation, and an unbounded first chunk puts the whole generation back on the clock. We flush at sentence end or every 12 words."
3 · One stream per segment "Each segment gets its own TTS stream, started as soon as the segment exists, so segment one is being synthesised and played while segment two is still being generated. With pooled connections, per-segment streams are cheap."
4 · Normalise before synthesis "Before synthesis, normalise the text. Tokens arrive split mid-word, so only complete words are released. Then a pronunciation lexicon maps terms like k8s to Kubernetes and etcd to E T C D. The transcript keeps the original text."
5 · What it measured "Measured: on a 32-word unpunctuated sentence, first audio went from 677 milliseconds with one stream to 437 with the 12-word flush."

real-time-systems-q10.testing: whether you can weigh a trending technology against control, observability and compliance, without dismissing it.

real-time-systems-q10.spoken:
Beat Say
1 · The honest answer "Not for us today, and the reason is specific to what we're building."
2 · What speech-to-speech wins "Native speech-to-speech models take audio in and produce audio out, so they remove the STT, LLM and TTS hops. That wins latency, and it keeps prosody, tone and emotion that a transcript throws away. For a conversational assistant that is a real upgrade."
3 · What the cascade keeps "What the cascade keeps is control and a record. In an interview product the transcript is the evidence: every score has to cite what the candidate said, verbatim, and a human has to be able to review it. The cascade also gives per-stage control where our product lives: keyterm prompting so technical terms survive, a pronunciation lexicon, an echo guard that drops our own voice before the record, and a rules-based Chair that decides which question comes next, so the model can't be talked out of the plan. And each stage is swappable and measurable on its own goldens."
4 · Where the line falls for us "So the honest 2026 answer is hybrid by path. Speech-to-speech could carry the conversational layer if it can be constrained to speak the planned question verbatim, while a parallel STT keeps the transcript of record and the scoring stays on text."
5 · What would change my mind "What would change my mind: if our turn budget can't be met with the cascade under load, the pipeline shape itself is the problem."
Close "Evidence and control decide it today; latency under load is what would reopen it."

real-time-systems-q11.spoken:
Beat Say
1 · The answer by path "It depends on the path. Real user audio over the public internet: WebRTC. Server-to-server audio where you control both ends and the network is good: a WebSocket is fine."
2 · Why TCP hurts live audio "The reason is TCP. A WebSocket runs on TCP, which must deliver every byte in order, so one lost packet stalls everything behind it: head-of-line blocking. For live speech you would rather drop a 20-millisecond frame and conceal it than stall and then burst."
3 · What WebRTC brings "WebRTC is UDP-based and built for media: a jitter buffer, packet-loss concealment, Opus with adaptive bitrate, ICE for getting through NATs, encryption, and, the one that decided it for us, browser-native echo cancellation, which only works on the capture path the browser controls."
4 · What it costs "The cost is complexity: signalling, ICE, STUN and TURN, more to operate. We took that complexity off our hands with LiveKit."
5 · What we did "In our system both are used: WebRTC between the candidate and the SFU and agent, and WebSockets from the agent to Deepgram for STT and TTS, which is a controlled server-to-server path from inside the region."
Close "WebRTC where the network is the user's, WebSocket where the network is ours."

real-time-systems-q12.spoken:
Beat Say
1 · Signalling "Four phases. Signalling first, and it isn't part of WebRTC: the two sides exchange an SDP offer and answer over a channel you provide, describing the media, codecs and encryption fingerprints."
2 · ICE gathers candidates "Then ICE gathers candidate addresses: host addresses on the local interface, server-reflexive addresses discovered through STUN, which is your public address as a NAT sees it, and relay addresses on a TURN server. Candidates are trickled to the other side through signalling."
3 · Connectivity checks "Then connectivity checks: ICE tries candidate pairs and picks one that works, preferring direct paths and falling back to TURN, which always works because it relays every byte, and always costs for the same reason. Some networks block UDP entirely, so TURN over TCP or TLS on 443 is the last resort."
4 · DTLS then SRTP "Once a pair is chosen, a DTLS handshake sets up keys and SRTP carries the encrypted media."
5 · Changes mid-call "Mid-call, a network change, wifi to cellular, triggers an ICE restart."
6 · How it looks with an SFU "With LiveKit it is the same protocol but a simpler shape: the client connects to the SFU over a signalling WebSocket with a token, negotiates with the SFU rather than with the agent, and the agent is another participant. LiveKit's built-in TURN covers the clients that can't reach the SFU directly."
Close "Signal, gather, check, encrypt, and expect a share of calls to be relayed."

real-time-systems-q13.spoken:
Beat Say
1 · Why TURN costs what it costs "TURN relays every byte of a call for clients that can't reach you directly, so it is priced by bandwidth and scales with concurrent relayed minutes, not with users."
2 · Measure the relay ratio "The number I watch is the relay ratio: the share of sessions whose selected ICE pair is a relay."
3 · Cut the rate "First I cut the rate: correct STUN so clients discover their public address, IPv6 where possible, and making sure the media server itself is reachable directly on UDP, so only clients behind restrictive NATs or firewalls relay."
4 · Cut the cost per relayed minute "Then the cost per relayed minute: region-local relays, and self-hosting where the volume justifies it."
5 · What we did "In our case the earlier stack was WebRTC with a self-hosted coturn relay, and it taught us one hard rule: anything holding live media state doesn't run on spot nodes. An evicted relay drops live calls, and an interview can't be re-run. When we moved to LiveKit, the SFU took the relay's place in the path and its built-in TURN covers the clients that can't reach it directly, so we stopped running coturn as a separate system. It is all in one Indian region, on on-demand nodes."

1 · Media absorbs it first "In layers. First the media stack absorbs it: the jitter buffer grows to smooth timing variance, which adds a little latency; packet-loss concealment fills lost frames; Opus lowers its bitrate; and redundant encoding helps with bursts. A few percent loss is mostly inaudible. LiveKit owns all of that."
2 · Then the transcript degrades "Second, the transcript degrades before the audio sounds bad: recognition confidence drops and words go missing. That is the part people forget, and in an interview it is a scoring problem. So the agent confirms more: a low-confidence turn gets a repeat request rather than being treated as a vague answer."
3 · Then the interview adapts "Third, the interview adapts. If quality stays poor, the agent acknowledges the line, slows its pacing and offers text: the candidate can finish by typing. That is a first-class path, not an error: the transcript is valid, the scoring works on text, and the scorecard records the modality so a human can weigh it."
4 · Disconnect and resume "If the connection drops, LiveKit reconnects and the interview state survives in the job process. If it can't reconnect, we save the turns, score the partial transcript, and offer to resume from the next question."
5 · What we measure "And I measure both layers: packet loss and reconnects, and how many sessions ended on text."
Close "Media absorbs, the transcript is protected, the interview adapts, and the state survives."

real-time-systems-q15.spoken:
Beat Say
1 · Voice breaks the stateless playbook "Voice sessions are stateful and long-lived, so the stateless autoscaling playbook doesn't apply: you can't move a live call to another pod, and a killed pod drops it."
2 · The order things break "In our planning, vendor concurrency and cost break first. At 1000 concurrent calls you hold 1000 streams each to STT, TTS and the LLM. If the TTS vendor starts queueing at a few hundred streams, first-audio latency climbs for everyone, and our TTS first byte is 55 percent of the turn budget. Second, the SFU topology: 2000 audio tracks is cheap bandwidth, but past a single node's comfortable limits, so it needs multi-node with Redis. Third, event-loop lag inside each call's process: a blocking call shows up as dead air. Last, node CPU and memory: linear and easy to buy."
3 · How each shows up "How it shows up: p95 first audio drifting up with concurrency while CPU stays low means a vendor is queueing you. Dispatch wait growing means the worker fleet is short. Loop-lag alerts mean a code problem, not a capacity one."
4 · What I'd check first "So I check vendor quotas first, and run one load test for interviews per pod."
5 · What never to do "What never to do: scale on CPU, scale from zero, or kill pods on deploy."
Close "Scale on concurrent sessions, keep warm capacity, and drain for the length of a call."

real-time-systems-q16.testing: backpressure for a producer you can't slow down, and whether you pick an overflow policy on purpose.
real-time-systems-q16.trap: an unbounded queue ("it'll catch up"), which becomes memory growth, growing lag and then an OOM.
real-time-systems-q16.spoken:
Beat Say
1 · The producer can't be paused "Audio is a real-time producer you can't pause: the person keeps talking whatever your consumer is doing."
2 · Bound the buffer "So the first rule is a bounded buffer with an explicit overflow policy. Unbounded means memory grows, lag grows with it, and eventually the process is killed."
3 · Drop stale, don't block "The policy depends on where you are. For audio headed to a live decision, stale audio is worthless: if you are 2 seconds behind, you would rather drop the oldest frames and catch up than process the backlog perfectly and reply late. For audio headed to a record, the transcript of an interview, dropping loses evidence, so you would rather apply backpressure upstream or spill to a durable buffer."
4 · Degrade deliberately "Then degrade deliberately: shed non-critical work first. In our current design that is built in: the analysis tier has deadlines and a budget, so under pressure it stops and the turn loop keeps going."
5 · Alert on depth "And alert on queue depth: a sustained backlog means you are under-provisioned, not momentarily unlucky."
6 · What I did "In the Deepgram pipeline I built, the fix was a bounded asyncio.Queue where the producer awaits put, which throttles it naturally instead of growing memory: <fill: the size N and how you picked it>."
Close "Bound it, choose the overflow policy on purpose, and treat depth as a capacity signal."

1 · Detect it "Degraded STT shows up two ways: slow, with interims and finals arriving late, or bad, with confidence dropping and words vanishing. I watch both per session: the interim interval, final latency, confidence, and empty transcripts while VAD says there is speech."
2 · Don't hang the turn "The turn must not hang on it. The STT stream has a timeout and a circuit breaker; if the stream stalls, the turn detector still has VAD, and the agent can say a short bridge line rather than sit in silence."
3 · Fail over or degrade "Failover mid-call is the hard part: the stream handle and the buffered audio have to move. A second provider needs its own warm connection and its own vocabulary list, and you accept losing the words in flight. If there is no second provider, degrade: ask the candidate to repeat, and if the problem persists, offer to continue by typing. The transcript stays valid either way."
4 · Say something honest "The spoken fallback must be honest, 'I'm having trouble hearing you', not silence."
5 · Protect the record "And the record: turns already committed are safe in the database, and the post-call scoring runs on whatever transcript exists, so a bad five minutes doesn't cost the whole interview."
Close "Detect per stream, never hang, degrade without restarting the call."

real-time-systems-q18.spoken:
Beat Say
1 · The meters "Stack the meters. STT bills per minute of audio streamed, whether anyone is speaking or not. TTS bills per character synthesised. The LLM bills per token. Then transport and compute: SFU and relay bandwidth, and a process per call for the whole session. Voice bills on time, not requests: an idle open call still costs."
2 · Why it grows within a call "And in a voice loop every turn re-sends context, so cost per turn grows through the call."
3 · Our shape of the bill "For our interviews there is a specific shape. The hot path is cheap. The analysis tier runs on every final phrase and restarts as the answer grows, and the design's speculative pre-generation is two to three times the analysis tokens, deliberately. The post-call panel is several strong-model reads of the full transcript, and at scale it dominates unit economics, so batching it and caching the rubric part of the prompt stop being optional."
4 · The levers "The levers: compact history, the speaker sees only the last eight messages, a smaller model for simple turns, caching fixed phrases, cutting the relay ratio, and budgets per run so a runaway call can't spend without limit."
5 · Model the tail "I'd model p50 and p99 cost per interview, because a long rambling call is the tail that hurts."

Beat Say
1 · Errors propagate silently "The danger is that recognition errors are silent: the next stage gets a confident, well-formed wrong string with no flag on it. So I treat recognised speech as untrusted input to any action, and stack cheap layers."
2 · Reduce the error at the source "At the source: tell the recogniser what to expect. Keyterm prompting and smart formatting help numbers come out as digits, and for a known ID format you can bias toward it. In our interview system smart formatting is on, because 300K QPS against three hundred K changes how a claim reads."
3 · Validate against the format "Validate against the format: length, prefix, check digit if the ID has one, and match against known values: does this policy exist for this caller? A wrong digit usually fails the checksum or the lookup."
4 · Confirm high-stakes slots "Confirm high-stakes slots by reading back: 'That's 4-7-1-2, is that right?' One extra turn, big error reduction. Low confidence always confirms; high stakes confirm regardless."
5 · Act only on confirmed values "Then act only on the final, committed and confirmed value, never on a partial. And for speaking it back, digits need to be spoken as digits, which is a TTS normalisation step."
Close "Recognised speech is untrusted input until it is validated and confirmed."

def luhn_ok(num: str) -> bool:
    total = 0
    for i, ch in enumerate(reversed(num)):
        d = int(ch) * (2 if i % 2 else 1)
        total += d - 9 if d > 9 else d
    return total % 10 == 0
print(luhn_ok("79927398713"))   # → True   (a valid test number)
print(luhn_ok("79927398718"))   # → False  (one digit misheard)

real-time-systems-q21.testing: that within-call memory is latency-critical, retrieval can't sit in the turn, and cross-call memory is written after the call.
real-time-systems-q21.trap: a synchronous vector search mid-turn that adds hundreds of ms to first audio.
real-time-systems-q21.spoken:
Beat Say
1 · Two horizons "Two horizons. Within the call, memory must be fast and complete enough to stay coherent. Across calls, it is retrieved and summarised, and written after the call, never on the hot path."
2 · Within the call "Within the call there are really three kinds of memory in our system. The conversation context for the speaker is compacted: it sees only the last eight messages, so the per-turn cost and latency don't grow through a 25-minute interview. The interview's progress is event-sourced: which questions were asked, how many probes were used, where we are in the plan, all computed from the moves the candidate actually heard, stored per turn. And the analysis results for each answer live in a per-interview context the turn logic reads."
3 · Retrieval off the critical path "Anything retrieved during the call must be pre-fetched: the plan, the keyterms, the candidate's profile are loaded before the first word. A search in the turn would blow the budget."
4 · Across calls "Across calls, things are written after the call: the Reviewer's per-question analysis, topic scores, and a revision ladder that moves a topic up or down. A resumed interview loads its earlier parts at the start, so the plan continues and the final evaluation covers every part."
5 · Memory must match what was heard "And memory must match what was heard: if Rachel was interrupted, the stored reply is the truncated one, or the agent remembers saying things nobody heard."

real-time-systems-q22.testing: whether you name PHI, consent and the clinical human-in-the-loop boundary, and turn noise and vocabulary into measured design choices.
real-time-systems-q22.trap: a generic voice-agent answer that never says PHI, consent or who commits a clinical action.
real-time-systems-q22.spoken:
Beat Say
1 · Clarify "First I'd clarify the users and the actions: is this patients at the bedside asking for help, or clinicians dictating and querying? And can it act, order, schedule, page, or only capture and inform? That decides everything about safety."
2 · Constraints and numbers "Constraints: protected health information is the hard one. So regional or on-premises inference, providers under a business associate agreement or equivalent, encryption in transit and at rest, redaction before anything is logged, zero-retention settings at every vendor, and consent and disclosure that it is an AI. I'd also switch off any framework's default recording; in my own system LiveKit Agents recorded to the cloud by default and we turned it off."
3 · Baseline design "The design is a cascaded pipeline, because hospitals need the transcript as a record: a near-field mic with echo cancellation and noise suppression; streaming STT with keyterm prompting from a drug and procedure lexicon; a semantic turn detector; a rules layer that decides what happens and a model that phrases it; TTS with a pronunciation lexicon for drug names."
4 · Deep-dive: the four asks "Noise: alarms, carts and other voices. Measure it. In my system a noise study showed steady noise cost only 3 to 4 points of term recall; vocabulary gaps cost far more. So vocabulary is the bigger lever: boost the formulary, validate recognised drug names against it, and confirm. For latency: co-locate media and inference in-region, keep connections warm, stream everything."
5 · Failure modes "And the safety line: clinical actions are human-in-the-loop. The assistant captures, reads back and queues; a clinician commits."
6 · What I'd reuse from my platform "From my own platform I'd reuse patterns, not code: rules that decide while a model only phrases, the vocabulary goldens, and text as a first-class fallback."
Close "PHI first, vocabulary before noise, and a clinician commits every action."

real-time-systems-q23.testing: that the unit of fairness is a concurrent session, and isolation is chosen per tier.
real-time-systems-q23.trap: request-rate limiting on a workload whose unit is a 45-minute session.
real-time-systems-q23.spoken:
Beat Say
1 · Noisy neighbours are audible "The difference is that noisy neighbours are immediate and audible: one tenant's spike degrades another tenant's live call, and you can't retry a live conversation."
2 · Concurrency caps, not rate limits "So limits are on concurrency, not request rate: each tenant gets a cap on concurrent sessions, and premium tiers get reserved capacity. That includes the vendor side: if the TTS vendor gives you 1000 streams, one tenant must not be able to take 900."
3 · Isolation by tier "Isolation is a spectrum: a shared pool is cheap and risky; dedicated worker pools per tier protect premium tenants; dedicated infrastructure or a region for regulated tenants."
4 · Per-tenant config runs deep "Per-tenant configuration runs deep in voice: the voice itself, prompts, vocabulary lists, pronunciation lexicon, escalation rules, data-residency region, retention. In our interview platform the rubric and its vocabulary come from the tenant's job description, so every session already loads a per-tenant keyterm list."
5 · Everything tenant-tagged "And every metric, log and trace is tenant-tagged, or you can't tell whose spike degraded whose calls. In our design the business gateway scopes every GraphQL resolver by tenant, and the agent's processes are per interview, which already isolates one call's crash or blocking bug from another's."
Close "Cap concurrency, isolate by tier, and tag everything by tenant."

real-time-systems-q24.testing: whether you treat audio, transcript and derived data as separate artifacts with separate rules, and whether you know your frameworks' defaults.
real-time-systems-q24.trap: "no, we don't record" while a framework silently does, or forgetting traces and indexes in deletion.
real-time-systems-q24.spoken:
Beat Say
1 · The answer for us "We keep the transcript, not the audio. The transcript is the evidence the scores cite, so it is needed. Raw audio adds risk, it is biometric-adjacent and carries accent and timbre, which our scoring must not use, for little benefit."
2 · Separate the artifacts "Then separate artifacts with separate rules. In our prototype the graph checkpoints, needed only during the call, are dropped an hour after it ends, 24 hours at most. Sessions with transcripts and scores are deleted after 30 days, with everything attached cascading. Profile and progress are kept because tracking over time is the point, and a person can be removed entirely. It runs every six hours."
3 · Consent and disclosure "Consent and disclosure are design elements: the greeting says it is an AI interviewer."
4 · Know every data flow "And 'we don't record' has to be checked, not assumed. LiveKit Agents, by default, records sessions to LiveKit Cloud: audio, transcript, traces and logs. We turned that off explicitly. The audio and text still reach our STT, LLM and TTS vendors for processing, so their retention settings and data agreements are part of the answer, and the consent screen should name them."
5 · Retention and erasure "And erasure has to reach every copy: the database, the checkpoints, and the traces. Our tracing tool keeps its own copy, which still needs a retention setting."
Close "Transcript, not audio; a rule per artifact; and deletion that reaches every copy."

real-time-systems-q25.testing: constraint first, a trade you made explicitly, what you rejected, and two numbers.
real-time-systems-q25.spoken:
Beat Say
1 · The decision it served "The product was an AI interviewer that holds a spoken technical interview, and its scores have to be valid."
2 · The constraint "The constraint: from the moment a candidate stops talking to the first sound of the next question, we had 800 milliseconds at p95. Past that it doesn't feel like a conversation, and candidates answer differently."
3 · Options weighed "The key decision was what owns turn-taking. The existing stack was hand-rolled WebRTC with a coturn relay, and our own endpointing design was a list of continuation words we admitted was guessed. I chose LiveKit, the SFU plus its agents runtime, self-hosted for production and LiveKit Cloud for the prototype, because it owns what dominates the budget: voice activity, a trained end-of-turn model, interruption handling, and one process per interview. The closest alternative was Pipecat; preferring it wouldn't have been wrong."
4 · What I built "Inside each interview process I split the agents by latency: rules pick the next move in about a millisecond; analysis agents run while the candidate is still talking; the real scoring happens after the call with independent assessors."
5 · What broke "What broke taught me the most. Our first TTS benchmark read 1.3 seconds; it was the harness, discarding pooled connections. Fixed, it was 319 milliseconds. The turn detector at 0.5 seconds cut people off mid-thought; 0.8 fixed it. Speech recognition turned 'idempotent' into 'item potent', which makes a strong candidate look vague: keyterms took term recall from about 80 percent to 89. And the agent's own voice through laptop speakers could be scored as the candidate's answer, so a guard drops it before the record."
6 · The number "In production: <fill: p50/p95 turn latency, concurrent sessions, one incident and what changed>."
Close "A latency constraint, a decision about who owns turn-taking, and four fixes with numbers."

real-time-systems-q26.testing: whether you can hold the whole system in your head, in order, and say why it's split the way it is, not just list components.
real-time-systems-q26.trap: starting with the tech stack ("we used LiveKit, Deepgram, LangGraph…"). Start with the constraint the stack serves.
real-time-systems-q26.spoken:
Beat Say
1 · The product constraint "It is an AI interviewer that runs a spoken technical interview, adapts its questions to the answers, and produces an evidence-backed scorecard afterwards. One constraint shapes everything: from the moment the candidate stops speaking to the first sound of the next question, we have 800 milliseconds at p95."
2 · Four tiers "So the system is split into four tiers, each with a different scaling axis. A small FastAPI control plane mints LiveKit tokens, creates rooms and handles webhooks; it never holds a live interview. A LiveKit SFU carries the audio over WebRTC. A LiveKit Agents worker fleet runs one process per interview, and that process holds the voice pipeline and the agent brain. And a cold path of queue workers does the heavy scoring after the call."
3 · One turn through the system "Inside one interview process, a turn goes like this: Silero VAD and Deepgram streaming STT listen to the candidate; LiveKit's turn-detection model decides whether they have finished or are just pausing; then the brain runs."
4 · The agents by latency tier "The brain is a LangGraph graph split by latency. The hot path is an intent guard and a rules-based Chair that picks the next move in about a millisecond, then a speaker agent that says it, streamed into TTS sentence by sentence. While the candidate is still talking, a warm tier, Assessor, Prober and Sentinel, analyses the answer so Chair has an insight ready at the end of the turn."
5 · After the call "When the call ends, two independent assessors score the full transcript, a reconciler resolves differences and a registrar writes the scorecard. In parallel, a Reviewer writes per-question feedback."
6 · What I'd defend and what's open "The principle I'd defend is that the design's hot path is transport, detection and synthesis, with no model generation. The honest caveat is that my prototype still has one streamed LLM call in the turn, which is the next thing to remove."
Close "One constraint, four tiers, and agents split by how fast they must answer."

stages.html:
Requirement Says Shapes
N1 candidate endpoint → first TTS byte: p50 ≤ 450 ms, p95 ≤ 800 ms ( design target) the hot path
N7 a completed interview must always produce a scorecard; a live interview can't be re-run the cold-path boundary

stages.name: Four tiers
stages.html:
Tier Runs Scales on Nodes
Control plane (FastAPI "Aditya") tokens, rooms, webhooks, session lifecycle requests (HPA) on-demand, small
Media (LiveKit SFU) WebRTC audio, built-in TURN tracks / connections on-demand, never spot
Agents (LiveKit Agents worker "Meghdootam") one subprocess per interview: VAD, STT, turn detection, brain, TTS concurrent interviews on-demand
Cold path (panel workers) scoring after the call queue depth (KEDA, scale to zero) spot

Fusing any two tiers forces the worse autoscaling behaviour of both. The spot rule comes from an earlier incident with the coturn relay: anything holding live media state never runs on spot nodes.

stages.html:
Prove it — the turn budget ( design):

turn detection            150–250 ms   LiveKit (vendor)
transcript → agent logic       ~5 ms   in-process
Chair selection                10 ms   ours (≈1 ms in the prototype)
text → first TTS chunk          5 ms   ours
TTS time to first byte        300 ms   TTS vendor (unverified under load)
SFU + network + jitter     60–120 ms   LiveKit
total                  530 typical / 690 p95   vs N1 p95 ≤ 800

Two vendor stages (turn detection + TTS first byte) are about 80% of it. That's where optimisation effort goes.

stages.name: The agents by latency tier
stages.claim: select in the turn, think around it
stages.html:
Tier When Who Kind
T0 every turn, ≤ 800 ms intent_guard → Chair → speaker (Chanakya) or a canned redirect rules, rules, LLM streamed
T1 while the candidate speaks, 2–20 s Assessor ∥ Prober ∥ Sentinel LLM, LLM, rules
T2 after the call, seconds to minutes Panel A ∥ B → Reconciler → Registrar, ∥ Reviewer LLM judges + code
  • Chair selects, never generates. If T1 isn't ready, Chair falls back to a word-count rule, so the candidate never waits on analysis.
  • The agent that asks never scores. Assessor's T1 score only steers; the Panel's T2 score is the one of record.

stages.name: After the call
stages.html:
After the call:Panel A ∥ Panel BReconcilerRegistrar writes the scorecard, with the Reviewer running in parallel
  • Two assessors get different framings and no shared context; the Reconciler resolves gaps over one point in favour of stronger verbatim evidence; the Registrar persists.
  • The Reviewer runs in parallel and never reads the Panel's output: per question it writes expected points, what was said, what was done well, what was missed and a model answer.
  • In the design, the cold path sits behind a queue (SQS) so a dead worker retries instead of losing the scorecard (N7). In the prototype, evaluation runs in the job process after the goodbye, with its own token budget, and publishes feedback_ready to the client.

stages.html:

interview.hint cant_hear
text streams on lk.transcription live captions

Not a second channel we run. See Q28.

dontSay: The stack as the answer ("LiveKit, Deepgram, LangGraph, GPT").
"The LLM decides what to ask" (Chair is rules; the speaker only phrases the move).
A designed number as if it were measured.

real-time-systems-q27.testing: whether you chose on the criterion that actually moves your product, and whether you can name the cost of your own choice.
real-time-systems-q27.trap: defending LiveKit on transport speed. Packet forwarding isn't measurable inside an 800 ms budget; turn-taking is.
real-time-systems-q27.spoken:
Beat Say
1 · The decision "We chose self-hosted LiveKit: the SFU for media and LiveKit Agents as the session runtime. Not LiveKit Cloud, and not a hand-rolled WebRTC stack."
2 · The constraint that forced it "The deciding criterion was: pick the thing that owns turn-taking, not the thing that forwards packets fastest. Two stages are about 80 percent of our turn budget, turn detection and TTS first byte, and a faster media server improves neither. What we needed was the agent runtime around the audio: voice activity detection, a trained end-of-turn model, interruption handling that flushes buffered audio correctly, and one process per interview. Our own endpointing design was a hand-written list of continuation words that we admitted was guessed."
3 · What we rejected "Self-hosted rather than Cloud because a live interview can't be re-run, so a completed interview must never lose its scorecard. I didn't want a commercial vendor in that media path, and per-minute pricing on 45-minute sessions is a real unit-economics line. The stack is Apache 2.0 and the turn model has open weights, so we can evaluate it on our accents. The closest alternative was Daily with Pipecat, and preferring that isn't wrong."
4 · What it cost "The honest costs: a third system to operate, multi-node with Redis is deferred work, and the turn model is English-only by LiveKit's own statement."
5 · What would reopen it "It reopens if self-hosting costs more than the Cloud licence, or the turn model fails on Indian English and fine-tuning doesn't fix it."
Close "Chosen for turn-taking, self-hosted for the scorecard, with the costs named."

Point What it means
Is LiveKit SFU (media, built-in TURN) + LiveKit Agents (job-per-interview runtime, VAD, turn detection, interruption, STT/TTS plugins).
Is not LiveKit Cloud; a media-only SFU with our own agent loop; hand-rolled WebRTC + coturn.
The seam LiveKit owns the conversational loop; LangGraph owns the decision made once per turn. Chair slots in where a LiveKit agent would call an LLM.

turn detection 250 + TTS first byte 300 = 550 of 690 ms p95  →  80%

stages.html:
Option Why not

LiveKit Cloud N7: vendor in the media path of an unrepeatable event; per-minute pricing (N3)

stages.claim: say it before they find it

upgrade cadence pin versions; re-run the regression set
a framework seam LangGraph must not also own control flow

  • A third system to operate. Coturn was already that tax, and LiveKit subsumes it, but at scale it wants Redis and multi-node config. Single node is fine through Phase 3; multi-node is deferred, not avoided.
  • Upgrade cadence. Agents moves fast: pin versions, treat an upgrade like a prompt change (re-run the regression set).
  • A framework seam. LiveKit Agents has its own orchestration; LangGraph must not also own control flow. The split above is the rule.

followUps.html:
The whole-stack story.

LiveKit Agents Pipecat

followUps.html:
No.

tens of nanoseconds per packet   against   a 700 ms budget   →   unmeasurable

It matters for a high-density relay. We run one candidate and one agent per room; our bottleneck is a 135M-parameter turn model and a TTS vendor.

followUps.question: How do you keep LiveKit upgrades from breaking interviews?
followUps.html:
Pin the version, and gate an upgrade like a prompt change.

upgrade proposedSTT and TTS goldensthe 25 manual call caseslatency on a real connectionship

Hook names in the Agents API move between releases; the division of responsibility is the stable part.

dontSay: "LiveKit is faster."
"We avoided vendor lock-in" without saying it's Apache 2.0 and self-hosted.
That Pipecat was a bad choice.

real-time-systems-q28.testing: that you know which traffic is loss-tolerant media and which is ordered, reliable control, and that you didn't build a second control channel you'd have to operate.
real-time-systems-q28.trap: "audio goes over WebRTC, everything else over our WebSocket server" — in this system there is no WebSocket server of ours; LiveKit's signalling socket carries the control messages.
real-time-systems-q28.spoken:
Beat Say
1 · The rule "The rule is: media goes over WebRTC, because it is UDP-based and built for live audio: jitter buffering, loss concealment, echo cancellation. Anything that must arrive complete and in order goes over a WebSocket, because TCP gives you that for free."
2 · The channel map "Concretely there are four WebSockets and one WebRTC path. The candidate's microphone and the agent's voice are Opus over RTP through the LiveKit SFU. The client's connection to LiveKit starts with a signalling WebSocket: join, SDP, ICE candidates, reconnects. The agent worker keeps its own WebSocket to LiveKit to register and receive job dispatches. And each interview process holds streaming WebSockets to Deepgram, for STT and for TTS. The only plain HTTP call is the client asking our FastAPI control plane for a token and a room."
3 · How the client learns state "That same signalling channel carries our control messages. The agent sets participant attributes for the interview phase, evaluating, paused, feedback ready, and a hint when it can't hear the candidate, and the live captions arrive as LiveKit text streams."
4 · The contract between repos "Between the client and server repos the shared surface is small: the token API and a small JSON schema, validated in CI on both sides."
5 · What breaks if mixed up "Why not our own WebSocket server for the control messages? Because it would be a second connection to keep alive, authenticate and reconnect, and its state could disagree with the room's."
Close "Using the room's own channel means the agent's state and the media share one lifecycle."

stages.name: The rule
stages.html:
WebRTC (UDP, RTP) WebSocket (TCP)
Delivery late packets dropped, concealed every byte, in order
Head-of-line blocking none one lost segment stalls what's behind it
Built in jitter buffer, PLC, AEC, adaptive bitrate nothing media-specific
Right for live mic and speaker audio signalling, state, captions, server-to-vendor streams

stages.name: The channel map
stages.html:
Channel Carries Protocol
Candidate ↔ SFU ↔ agent mic audio up, agent TTS down WebRTC: Opus/RTP, DTLS-SRTP, ICE, TURN in LiveKit
Client ↔ LiveKit join, SDP, ICE, reconnect; attributes; text streams LiveKit signalling WebSocket
Worker ↔ LiveKit "available for jobs", job dispatch worker WebSocket
Job process ↔ Deepgram streaming STT (interims, finals) and TTS WebSockets, pooled per session
Client → FastAPI token, room, agent dispatch HTTPS POST

stages.name: How the client learns state
stages.html:
Prove it — the messages as the client sees them ( prototype):

participant attributes (set by the agent, read by the client)
  interview.phase = "evaluating"        → show "Preparing your feedback"
  interview.phase = "feedback_ready"    + interview.session_id → open the review page
  interview.phase = "paused"            → resumable, not evaluated yet
  interview.hint  = "cant_hear"         → user state "away": mic muted or wrong device
  interview.hint  = ""                  → cleared when speech is heard again
text stream, topic "lk.transcription"   → live caption bubbles, both speakers
  • Attributes are state, not events: a client that reconnects reads the current value instead of replaying a missed message.
  • The cant_hear hint exists because a muted mic otherwise looks like a stuck "Listening" screen.

stages.name: The contract between repos
stages.html:
Shared surface Form
the token API OpenAPI
data messages a small JSON schema, mirrored in both repos and validated in CI
  • Client and server are separate repos. Once LiveKit owned signalling, the shared surface collapsed to two things: the token API (OpenAPI) and a small JSON schema for data messages.
  • Both repos validate against the mirrored schema in CI. The failure to design against is a client sending a field the agent silently ignores.
  • Open question: where the canonical schema lives (shared package, submodule or code generation).

stages.name: What breaks if mixed up
stages.html:
Mix-up Failure
audio over a WebSocket from a browser one lost TCP segment stalls every frame behind it; you rebuild jitter buffering and lose browser AEC
control over a lossy data channel without acks a dropped feedback_ready leaves the client waiting forever

Attributes avoid the second: the latest value is state that survives reconnects.

followUps.question: Why do vendor streams use WebSockets and not WebRTC?
followUps.html:
Server-to-server on a good network, with both ends under control.

WebRTC feature Needed there?
NAT traversal, echo cancellation no
what matters instead a warm connection: a cold TLS connect to Deepgram from India measured ~620 ms , so connections are pooled and opened before first speech

followUps.question: "WebSockets are real-time, so they're fine for audio."
followUps.html:
Real-time delivery isn't the issue; ordering is.

  • TCP must deliver in order, so under loss the audio stalls and then bursts.
  • For live speech you would rather drop a late 20 ms frame and conceal it.

followUps.question: The client reconnects mid-interview. What does it miss?
followUps.html:
Nothing the scorer uses.

Thing After a reconnect
media LiveKit's job: ICE restart, signalling reconnect
phase attributes are re-read on rejoin, so it is correct
captions sent while disconnected lost from the live view; the transcript of record is server-side

followUps.question: Would you ever add your own WebSocket server?
followUps.html:
Only for traffic that isn't tied to the room's lifecycle.

Traffic Channel
a dashboard of past interviews with live updates our own server would be fine
anything inside an interview the room's channel: a second one means a second auth, a second reconnect path and two sources of truth

followUps.question: How is the token protected?
followUps.html:
The API secret never reaches the browser.

FastAPI mints a short-lived JWTscoped to one room and identitypublish, subscribe and data grantsplus the agent dispatch, so the right worker joins

spine: What's ready before the first word
real-time-systems-q29.testing: whether you understand that a voice agent is a participant dispatched into a room, not an HTTP handler, and how the plan reaches it safely.
real-time-systems-q29.trap: "the client calls our API, which starts the agent." Nothing calls the agent; LiveKit dispatches a job when the candidate joins.
real-time-systems-q29.spoken:
Beat Say
1 · The one-line flow "The client asks our FastAPI control plane for a token, connects to LiveKit with it, and LiveKit dispatches the agent into the room when the candidate joins. Nothing calls the agent."
2 · The token carries the dispatch "The control plane checks the candidate owns the interview plan they are starting, names a fresh room server-side, and mints a short-lived LiveKit JWT: one room, one identity, publish and subscribe grants, and a room configuration that says dispatch the agent named meghdootam into this room, with metadata: the candidate ID, the plan ID, and whether this continues a paused interview. Because the metadata is signed into the token, the agent can trust it."
3 · The worker and the job "When the client joins, LiveKit creates the room and dispatches a job to an available agent worker. The worker is a long-running process registered with LiveKit over a WebSocket. It has idle subprocesses that are already prewarmed: Silero VAD is loaded before any job arrives."
4 · What's ready before the first word "The job lands in one of them, reads the metadata, loads the plan, builds the keyterm list for STT from that plan, and starts the session. The agent speaks first."
5 · Why it's built this way "Two properties I wanted: the agent never arrives before the candidate, so there is no greeting to an empty room; and the plan is known before STT is configured, so the vocabulary boost is right from the first word."
Close "A signed token carries the dispatch, and the agent joins as a participant."

stages.name: The one-line flow
stages.claim: five hops, one of them HTTP

stages.name: The token carries the dispatch
stages.html:
Prove it — what the token holds ( prototype, simplified):

identity   cand-<12 hex>            stable per person, reveals nothing
ttl        30 min                   to join, not the interview length
grants     room_join, room=interview-<8 hex>, can_publish, can_subscribe, can_publish_data
room_config.agents = [ RoomAgentDispatch(
    agent_name = "meghdootam",
    metadata   = {"candidate_id": …, "plan_id": …, "continue_from": …} ) ]
  • Server-named room for prepared interviews: a client can't pick a room name that collides with someone else's (threat model T8).
  • Ownership check first: someone else's plan returns the same error as a missing one, so plan IDs can't be probed.

stages.name: The worker and the job
stages.html:
Dispatch:worker registers under an agent namecandidate joinsLiveKit dispatches a joban idle, prewarmed subprocess runs the interview
  • The worker registers under an explicit agent name, which also turns off automatic dispatch into every room.
  • LiveKit dispatches on join; the worker hands the job to an idle subprocess. #processes = #concurrent interviews.
  • Prewarm runs once per idle subprocess before any job: model load (hundreds of ms) stays off the first turn.

stages.name: What's ready before the first word
stages.html:
Step in entrypoint Why before the first turn
parse metadata → load the plan Chair needs it at turn 0
continuing? load earlier parts Chair skips questions already asked; evaluation covers all parts
build ≤ 100 keyterms from plan, topics, sections, stack STT is configured once, at session start
start the interview's model budget (calls, tokens) a runaway loop hits a hard stop, not a bill
open checkpoints, build the graph per-turn state keyed by turn

stages.html:
Alternative Failure it has
a pre-created room and a separate dispatch a worker restart between the two misses the dispatch
the agent joins first it greets an empty room, or the candidate misses the opening
the plan fetched after the session starts STT runs the first answer without the domain vocabulary

The candidate joins a room with no agent, and the client says so.
client shows "Waiting for the interviewer"

alert on dispatch wait time

followUps.html:
The TTL bounds when the token can be used to join.

  • Once connected, the session isn't cut at expiry.
  • Reconnects are handled by LiveKit.

Then any client could run any plan against any candidate record.

Wrong:client names the planagent trusts it
Right:server checks ownershipsigns plan and candidate ID into the tokenagent reads the token

followUps.html:
Open question, to decide at integration.

Option Consequence
the Spring gateway mints tokens (LiveKit has a Java server SDK) the FastAPI edge might not need to exist
keep the edge watch it growing features one reasonable step at a time

A room name chosen by the client for a prepared interview.

real-time-systems-q30.testing: whether you know the difference between a request/response server and a long-lived stateful session, and where each belongs.
real-time-systems-q30.trap: "we run each interview in a FastAPI background task" — one blocking call then stalls every interview on that worker.
real-time-systems-q30.spoken:
Beat Say
1 · The decision "Because an interview isn't a request. It is a 45-minute stateful session with a soft real-time loop inside it, so it runs in LiveKit Agents: a worker registers with LiveKit, and each interview runs as its own job in its own process. There are three runtime shapes on the server: the agent worker, the panel worker that scores after the call from a queue, and FastAPI."
2 · The constraint "FastAPI's concurrency model doesn't give you one unit per interview. Uvicorn gives you worker processes with one async event loop each. Put ten interviews on one worker and they share one event loop; one blocking STT or LLM call, or a sync SDK someone added, stalls turn-taking for all ten. The symptom isn't an error, it is dead air on ten live calls."
3 · What we rejected "So I rejected interviews as background tasks or WebSocket handlers, and agent logic behind HTTP endpoints, which adds a hop to every turn."
4 · What it cost "FastAPI is the one that really is request and response: it mints tokens, creates rooms, handles webhooks and serves past interviews. It is stateless, off the media path, and three to six replicas cover a thousand concurrent interviews. The cost is more moving parts, and the thing to watch is that service slowly growing features that belong elsewhere."
5 · What would reopen it "It reopens when the voice service meets the wider platform: the Spring gateway could mint tokens, and the FastAPI edge could disappear."
Close "A session runtime for sessions, a request server for requests."

stages.name: The decision
stages.claim: three runtime shapes, one is FastAPI
stages.html:
# Process Shape Trigger Lifetime
1 Agent worker LiveKit Agents worker job dispatch on room join one job per interview, up to 45 min
2 Panel worker queue consumer SQS message () seconds to minutes
3 Control plane FastAPI HTTP from the client milliseconds

stages.name: The constraint
stages.html:
Prove it — what one blocking call does to a shared loop (illustrative):

10 interviews on one uvicorn worker, one event loop
one sync call blocks the loop for 400 ms
→ every interview on that worker misses its turn deadline by up to 400 ms
→ 400 ms is half the 800 ms p95 budget, on ten calls at once
with a process per interview: the same bug costs one call 400 ms

stages.name: What we rejected
stages.html:
Option Why not
interviews as FastAPI background tasks / WebSocket handlers shared event loop; deploys kill live calls; no drain semantics for 45-min sessions
agent logic behind HTTP endpoints the voice loop calls adds a network hop to every turn, and the endpoint becomes a stateless shell around state that lives elsewhere

stages.name: What it cost
stages.claim: three processes and a scope rule
stages.html:
Cost Guard
three things to deploy and observe agent and panel worker are one image with a MODE switch
FastAPI's scope creeping a rule, reviewed: each added feature looks reasonable by itself
a webhook storm at peak idempotent and fast: return 200, enqueue heavy work
  • Three things to deploy and observe instead of one. Two of them (agent and panel worker) are one image with a MODE switch, so they can't drift apart in version.
  • FastAPI's scope is a rule, not a guarantee: session creation, candidate lookup, scorecard reads each look reasonable. Webhooks must stay idempotent and fast (return 200, enqueue heavy work) or a webhook storm at peak becomes the bottleneck.

stages.name: What would reopen it
stages.html:
At platform integration Outcome
the Spring gateway mints tokens (LiveKit has a Java SDK) the FastAPI edge disappears
the edge ships as a third MODE of the same image one deployment fewer
  • When the voice service meets the wider platform: LiveKit has a Java SDK, so the Spring gateway could mint tokens and the FastAPI edge could disappear. Or the edge ships as a third MODE of the same image instead of its own deployment.

followUps.question: Couldn't you use asyncio.to_thread for blocking calls and stay in FastAPI?
followUps.html:
That discipline is applied inside the agent process too; it doesn't fix the structure.

Still true inside FastAPI
interviews on one worker share a loop
deploys kill live calls
a 45-minute session has no drain

Process isolation makes the discipline a mitigation, not the only defence.

followUps.question: "FastAPI is async, so it handles thousands of concurrent connections."
followUps.html:
Thousands of idle connections, yes.
it handles many idle connections
it doesn't isolate soft real-time loops doing VAD on 30 ms frames and streaming to three vendors each

Concurrency isn't the same as isolation.

followUps.question: How do you deploy the agent without killing live calls?
Where does session state live, if not in FastAPI?
followUps.html:
In the agent job process, and in Postgres for anything durable.

State Where
live graph checkpoints keyed by turn, in-memory insights
durable Postgres
FastAPI reads Postgres to serve past interviews; never holds a live one

dontSay: "FastAPI can't scale."
That the choice was about Python vs another language.

spine: The six stages after the endpoint
real-time-systems-q31.testing: a per-stage budget with owners, and whether you know which work happens before the endpoint so it isn't on the clock.
real-time-systems-q31.trap: starting the clock at "the candidate speaks" or quoting one total number.
real-time-systems-q31.spoken:
Beat Say
1 · Where the clock starts "The clock starts at the endpoint, the moment the system decides the candidate has finished, and stops at the first audio byte reaching them. Our target is 450 milliseconds at p50 and 800 at p95."
2 · What already happened during speech "A lot happens before the clock starts. While the candidate is speaking, Deepgram streams interim transcripts, and each final phrase kicks off the warm tier, Assessor, Prober and Sentinel, so by the endpoint there is usually already an insight for this answer."
3 · The six stages after the endpoint "Then six stages. The turn detector confirms they are done: 150 to 250 milliseconds. The transcript reaches the brain in-process, about 5. The intent guard and Chair pick the move: rules, 10 in the budget. The text goes to TTS in sentence-sized chunks, 5. The TTS vendor produces the first audio: 300. And the SFU, network and jitter buffer add 60 to 120. That is about 530 typical, 690 at p95, and two stages are 80 percent of it."
4 · Where the prototype differs "Where my prototype differs: the speaker agent is still an LLM that phrases the move, so model time to first token sits inside the turn. From India that measured around 850 milliseconds for every OpenAI model we tried. LiveKit's preemptive generation hides part of it; removing it with speculative pre-generation is the next step."
5 · How I measure it "I measure it per turn and per stage, on a real connection, never localhost."
Close "The clock starts at the endpoint, and two vendor stages own most of it."

stages.html:
The clock:last wordendpoint decided (the clock starts)move selectedfirst TTS byte at the candidate (the clock stops)
  • N1: endpoint → first TTS byte, p50 ≤ 450 ms, p95 ≤ 800 ms ().
  • The endpoint is a decision (the turn detector's), so part of its cost is inside the budget: the silence it waits for.
  • Everything that can run during speech must run during speech.

stages.html:
During speech Cadence Result
Deepgram interims ~300 ms live captions, preemptive generation input
Final phrase → T1 (Assessor ∥ Prober ∥ Sentinel) debounced 300 ms, restarted on each new phrase insights[turn] ready by the endpoint, often
Diarization labels per phrase second-voice signal for Sentinel

Prove it — the timeline ( design budget):

t (ms) Event Owner
0 last word; silence begins candidate
150–250 turn detector commits the turn LiveKit (VAD + EOU model)
+5 final transcript into the graph in-process
+10 intent_guard → Chair selects the move ours, rules
+5 first sentence chunk dispatched ours

+60–120 SFU forward, network, jitter buffer LiveKit

stages.name: Where the prototype differs
stages.claim: one LLM call still in the turn
stages.html:
Design Prototype
Speaker Chair picks a pre-rendered NextMove; no generation Chanakya (LLM) writes a short acknowledgement, then the planned question verbatim
LLM in the turn none one streamed call; OpenAI TTFT ~850 ms from India (, network-bound)
Hiding it speculative pre-generation during speech LiveKit preemptive generation: starts before end-of-turn is confirmed, discarded if speech continues

The honest statement: the prototype does not meet the design budget, and I can name the two reasons.

stages.name: How I measure it
stages.html:
Logged On
e2e, llm_ttft, tts_ttfb every agent turn
stt_delay, eou_delay every user turn
alert endpoint_to_first_byte p95 > 800
  • Every agent turn logs e2e, llm_ttft, tts_ttfb; every user turn logs stt_delay and eou_delay (end-of-turn delay).
  • The alert: endpoint_to_first_byte p95 > 800 ().
  • Latency claims come from a real connection, never localhost: local runs omit the SFU hop and residential networks.

followUps.question: Which stage would you attack first?
followUps.html:
The biggest controllable one.

In Attack first
the design TTS first byte: verify the vendor's real number under load, then region
the prototype the in-turn LLM call, by moving generation into speech time

followUps.question: Raise min_delay from 0.8 s to 1.2 s. What changes?
followUps.html:
Up to 400 ms more latency on finished-sounding turns, for fewer split answers.

min_delay Median latency Thinking pauses cut in two
0.8 s baseline more
1.2 s up to 400 ms higher fewer

Decide it on measured cut-off rates, not feel.

followUps.question: "Just use a faster LLM."
followUps.html:
It is network-bound, not model-bound.

  • Measured **:** ~850 ms TTFT for every OpenAI model from India; LiveKit's inference gateway wasn't faster.
  • The fix is structural: don't generate inside the turn.

followUps.question: Why does network sit at the end and not the start?
followUps.html:
The uplink happens during speech.

Leg On the clock?
uplink of the candidate's audio no: it overlaps their speech
downlink of the first audio (SFU forward, internet path, jitter buffer) yes

followUps.question: How would you show a hiring panel this works?
followUps.html:
A live per-turn waterfall on a real residential connection.

It is the Phase 1 exit criterion, and worth more than any UI.

dontSay: "About half a second" with no breakdown.
That the prototype has no LLM in the turn.

real-time-systems-q32.testing: whether you'll own a gap between your design and your code, and whether you understand speculative pre-generation well enough to say why it's hard.
real-time-systems-q32.trap: defending the contradiction ("it's only a small call"). Concede first, then show you know the way out and why you sequenced it later.
real-time-systems-q32.spoken:
Beat Say
1 · Concede it "You're right, and it is the main deviation from the design: the prototype has one streamed LLM call in every turn."
2 · Why the design forbids it "The design's rule is that nothing in the turn generates: the warm tier drafts two to four candidate next moves while the candidate is still talking, fully rendered, and at the endpoint Chair just picks one in about ten milliseconds. The reason is arithmetic. Human tolerance for silence is around 800 milliseconds, and a model call from India measured about 850 to first token by itself. It can't fit."
3 · What the prototype does instead "The prototype keeps Chair as pure rules, but the speaker agent is an LLM that phrases Chair's move. On an ask move I constrained it hard: it may write a short acknowledgement, dropped if it is over ten words or contains a question, and then the planned question is spoken verbatim, so scoring stays valid. Two things hide the cost: LiveKit's preemptive generation starts the speaker before the endpoint is confirmed, and sentence chunking lets the first sentence reach TTS while the rest is generated."
4 · What it costs today "The cost is that the prototype doesn't meet the design budget, and I say so."
5 · The path out "Why not build speculation first? Because it depends on things that weren't defined: what counts as a speculative hit, the phase machine, the steering algorithm. Building it before those exist means rebuilding it."
Close "Conceded, constrained, and sequenced on purpose."

stages.name: Concede it
stages.claim: one streamed LLM call per turn
stages.html:
Design Prototype
Chair selects among pre-rendered NextMoves selects a move kind by rules (~1 ms)
Text written during speech by the warm tier written in the turn by Chanakya, streamed
Guard "if generation enters the §10 table, the design has regressed" known deviation, documented in hot_path.py

stages.name: Why the design forbids it
stages.html:
Prove it — the arithmetic:

design turn without generation     ~690 ms p95
measured OpenAI TTFT from India    ~850 ms  (network-bound; LiveKit Inference no faster)
690 − 10 (Chair) + 850             ≈ 1,530 ms if generation were fully on the clock
N1 p95 target                         800 ms
  • The design's answer: speculative pre-generation. T1 produces a ranked set of NextMove objects (utterance, targets, confidence, generated_for_turn) during speech; Chair picks with a staleness and confidence check.
  • The fallback ladder when nothing fresh exists: best speculative move → next plan-order question → a bridge utterance that buys ~1.5 s.

stages.name: What the prototype does instead
stages.html:
Technique What it does
constrain on ask: an acknowledgement of ≤ 10 words, then the planned question verbatim
overlap preemptive_generation starts before end-of-turn is confirmed
chunk the first sentence, or 12 words, goes to TTS at once
Point What it means
Constrain the output on ask, the LLM writes only an acknowledgement (≤ 10 words, no question mark) and the planned question follows verbatim. The plan, T1 and the Panel all assume that exact question was asked.
Overlap preemptive_generation starts the brain on the transcript before end-of-turn is confirmed; if the candidate continues, the result is discarded. Every graph write is keyed by turn and overwritten, so a re-run is idempotent.
Chunk the first sentence (or 12 words) goes to TTS as soon as it exists.
Only the speaker speaks LangGraph runs with stream_mode="custom", so only text a node writes through the stream writer reaches TTS, never an internal classification call.

stages.name: What it costs today
stages.html:
Cost today Detail
latency median turn above the design target, dominated by model TTFT
tokens preemptive generation is wasted when the candidate keeps talking
dependency every turn needs the LLM provider up; no model-free speaker yet
a buffered acknowledgement a few words held back so they can be checked
  • Median turn latency above the design target, dominated by model TTFT.
  • Preemptive generation wastes tokens when the candidate keeps talking; it's a cheap version of speculation, without ranking or confidence.
  • Every turn depends on the LLM provider being up. A circuit breaker makes an outage fail fast instead of waiting on timeouts, but the prototype has no model-free speaker yet; the design's answer is the plan-order question and the bridge utterance, which need no generation.
  • On an ask, the acknowledgement is buffered (a few words) so it can be checked before anything is spoken. That's a small, deliberate latency cost for scoring validity.

stages.name: The path out
stages.html:
Path out:define the hit metricrender utterances in T1 during speechChair selects, the speaker becomes a lookupexit at hit rate ≥ 70%
  1. Define speculative_hit_rate. The cheap definition (a move passed staleness and confidence checks) and the meaningful one (a human would have chosen it too) differ; pick before building.
  2. Move Chanakya's phrasing into T1: render the utterance for the likely next moves during speech.
  3. Chair selects; the speaker node becomes a lookup.
  4. Exit criterion ( Phase 4): hit rate ≥ 70% and the turn budget met on a residential connection.

followUps.html:
Yes, deliberately: 2–3× the T1 tokens.

If the unit economics come back badly
do fewer candidates per turn
don't abandon speculation

The cost is unquantified today; that is an open item.

followUps.html:
Every move is stamped, and Chair rejects stale ones.

Check Rejects

followUps.html:

Change Helps

followUps.html:
The preemptive result is discarded.

turn not committedresult discardedthe brain runs again on the longer transcriptthe graph write for that turn is overwritten

followUps.question: Would you ship to real candidates like this?
followUps.html:
For practice, yes; for hiring decisions, not until the budget is met.

Use Ship?
