hiring decisions after the budget is met: a slow interviewer changes how candidates answer, which is a fairness question

dontSay: "There's no LLM in the hot path" about the prototype.
"It's only one call."

real-time-systems-q33.testing: whether you know VAD, endpointing and turn detection are different things, and whether your settings came from evidence.
real-time-systems-q33.trap: "we use a 500 ms silence timeout". No fixed hangover works for people who pause to think.
real-time-systems-q33.spoken:
Beat Say
1 · The decision "Three different signals. Silero VAD answers whether there is speech in this 30-millisecond frame. Endpointing answers whether this utterance has ended. Turn detection answers the harder question: has this person finished their turn, or are they pausing to think. We use LiveKit's end-of-turn model for that: a small transformer that reads the recent words together with the audio. The settings: wait at least 0.8 seconds of silence when the turn sounds finished, and up to 3.5 when the model thinks they are mid-thought."
2 · The constraint "No fixed silence threshold works for people who pause to think. We started at 0.5 seconds and it cut people off at thinking pauses, so we raised it. In an interview a cut-off answer reads as vaguer, so it is a fairness issue."
3 · What we rejected "Vendor endpointing in Deepgram is off. Two end-of-turn authorities would fight, one committing a turn the other thinks is still open. Deepgram still gets a finalize signal when VAD says speech ended, so the final transcript arrives on time. That is a deviation from LiveKit's own advice, which is STT endpointing by default."
4 · What it cost "The weak point: the model is English-only by LiveKit's statement, and we haven't measured it on Indian English yet. And 0.8 seconds is slower than the design budget assumes."
5 · What would reopen it "The fallback is a tuned fixed hangover, not a return to hand-written transport."
Close "One semantic authority for the end of a turn, tuned from what we saw, with the language gap named."

stages.name: The decision
stages.html:
Signal Question Ours
VAD speech in this frame? Silero, ~1 ms per 30 ms chunk, prewarmed per process
Endpointing did the utterance end? vendor endpointing off (endpointing_ms=0)
Turn detection (EOU) did the turn end? LiveKit model: 135M params (SmolLM v2 base), ~50 ms inference, four-turn window (LiveKit)

Prove it — the prototype settings, annotated ():

turn_detection = TurnDetector()          # audio + words, "finished" vs "pausing"
endpointing    = { min_delay: 0.8 s,     # silence before a finished-sounding turn commits
                   max_delay: 3.5 s }    # longest wait when the model says "mid-thought"
stt.endpointing_ms = 0                   # one authority; plugin still sends Finalize on VAD end

stages.name: The constraint
stages.html:
Fixed hangover Effect
150 ms fast, interrupts anyone who pauses to think
250 ms still cuts mid-sentence pauses
500 ms+ never interrupts, feels slow and dead

In an interview, cutting a candidate off mid-thought isn't only a UX problem: the split answer reads as vaguer to the scorer, and vagueness is what the Prober probes. That makes it a fairness issue.

stages.name: What we rejected
stages.html:
Rejected Why
v0.1: an adaptive hangover from a hand-written list of continuation words the list was guessed, not derived from recorded speech
STT endpointing (LiveKit's default recommendation) acoustics and punctuation alone; beside the EOU model it makes two authorities
endpointing tuned per question type useful in task bots; the semantic model gets most of it from the words
  • v0.1 design: an adaptive hangover driven by a hand-written list of continuation words. Our own open questions flagged the list as guessed, not derived from recorded speech. Withdrawn.
  • STT endpointing (LiveKit's default recommendation): simpler, but the vendor decides on acoustics and punctuation alone, and running it alongside the EOU model gives two authorities.
  • Endpointing tuned per question type ("expect a long pause after 'my policy number is'"): useful in task bots; the semantic model gets most of it from the words.

stages.name: What it cost
stages.html:
Cost Detail
English-only (LiveKit) no published data on Indian English or Hinglish; not yet measured by us
turn splits still happen "I'm Prathap, a / pen engineer": a split costs a restarted reply, not a skipped question
0.8 s is slower than the 150–250 ms the design budget assumes
  • English-only (LiveKit): no published data on Indian English or Hinglish. Open weights mean we can evaluate and fine-tune; nobody has measured it yet.
  • Turn splits still happen. A live test cut "backend engineer" at a pause ("I'm Prathap, a / pen engineer"). Chair treats a paused answer as one answer (the warm tier re-analyses all committed turns since the last full reply), so a split costs a restarted reply, not a skipped question.
  • 0.8 s is slower than the 150–250 ms the design budget assumes. It's the right trade for thinking pauses, and it moves latency.

stages.name: What would reopen it
stages.html:
Measurement Then
cut-off rate by accent cohort degrades on Indian English, and fine-tuning doesn't fix it a tuned fixed hangover; the transport decision doesn't change
median latency matters more than cut-offs (a support bot) revisit STT endpointing

A cut-off is a turn followed within a second by more speech from the candidate.

  • Measure cut-off rate (a turn followed within a second by more speech from the candidate) by accent cohort. If the model degrades on Indian English and fine-tuning doesn't fix it, switch to a tuned fixed hangover; the transport decision doesn't change.
  • If median turn latency matters more than cut-offs for a product (a support bot), revisit STT endpointing.

followUps.question: Is barge-in also governed by the turn detector?
followUps.html:
No.

Governed by
barge-in acoustic onset: VAD, 0.4 s of voice while the agent speaks
turn completion the turn detector

A candidate interrupting must be heard whatever they are saying.

followUps.html:
That was our first design, and the rules were a guess.

  • Adaptive on what? The signal that separates finished from pausing is mostly in the words and prosody.
  • That is what the model is trained on.

followUps.html:
The model reads "um…" as unfinished and waits.

"um…"VAD sees silencewait past min_delay, up to max_delay 3.5 sresume inside it: one turn

Past 3.5 s the turn commits, and what follows is re-analysed as part of the same answer.

followUps.html:
Three readings, and the fairness one decides.

Measure From

followUps.question: Why is the model's language support a fairness issue and not just quality?
followUps.html:
Because cut-offs aren't random.

a speaker the model wasn't trained onmore cut-offsa cut-off answer scores worse

dontSay: "VAD tells us when they've finished."
That the English-only limit is solved.

spine: Decide what the move was worth
Treat the answer as one answer
real-time-systems-q34.testing: that you know the framework handles the audio, and that you own the bookkeeping: what the candidate actually heard, and what that means for the plan and the score.
real-time-systems-q34.trap: stopping at "we stop the TTS". The hard part is the record afterwards.
real-time-systems-q34.spoken:
Beat Say
1 · Detect on sound "Detection is on sound, not words. LiveKit's interruption handling in VAD mode fires when there is at least 0.4 seconds of candidate voice while Rachel is speaking. Waiting for a transcript would add 200 to 300 milliseconds, and the candidate would hear Rachel talk over them."
2 · Stop the audio "The framework then stops consuming the TTS stream and flushes the audio already queued, so the tail doesn't keep playing."
3 · Record what was heard "It appends to the conversation what was actually spoken, truncated and marked interrupted, not what was generated."
4 · Decide what the move was worth "The bookkeeping is ours, because it has scoring consequences. Chair tracks progress as a fold over moves the candidate actually heard. An interrupted probe or clarification didn't happen: it doesn't spend the probe budget and doesn't advance the plan. An interrupted ask counts only if the planned question itself was fully spoken before they cut in."
5 · Treat the answer as one answer "Everything the candidate says after the last move they heard is treated as one answer, so a barge-in doesn't split their answer into fragments the Assessor scores separately."
6 · Tell noise from interruption "Finally, not every sound is an interruption. If no words arrive within two seconds, a cough or a desk tap, Rachel resumes where she stopped and no candidate turn is created. Backchannels under 0.4 seconds don't trigger it at all."
Close "The framework owns the audio; we own what the record and the plan keep."

stages.name: Detect on sound
stages.claim: VAD, 0.4 s, while the agent speaks
stages.html:
Detect:candidate voice for 0.4 s while Rachel speaksinterruption fires on soundthe transcript follows 200–300 ms later
Point What it means
Why not the transcript it arrives 200–300 ms after the sound. By then the agent has spoken over the candidate.
Why 0.4 s long enough to ignore a short backchannel or a click, short enough to feel responsive.
Mode vad, not LiveKit's adaptive (an ML model that ignores backchannels). vad makes barge-in predictable and visible while tuning; adaptive is the candidate for production once measured.

stages.name: Stop the audio
stages.html:
Buffer What's in it Action
TTS stream audio still being synthesised stop consuming it
outbound pacing buffer audio synthesised but not yet sent flush
client playout audio already sent the stream ends; nothing new arrives

v0.1 of our design specified this sequence by hand. It's the class of detail that's easy to get subtly wrong, so it's now the framework's.

stages.name: Record what was heard
stages.html:
Prove it — two turns in the stored shape (illustrative text):

turn 7  assistant  "That makes sense. How would you shard the led…"   interrupted=1
turn 8  user       "Sorry, one second — by account id, and…"          interrupted=0
  • The history holds what was heard, not what was generated.
  • The design goes further: record the exact character offset reached in the TTS stream, so the Assessor never penalises an answer to a question that wasn't fully asked.

stages.name: Decide what the move was worth
stages.html:
def delivered(move, spoken, plan):          # 🔧 hot_path.py, abridged
    done, text = spoken                     # (spoken to the end?, text heard)
    if done or move["kind"] == "greet":
        return True
    if move["kind"] == "ask":               # did the planned question itself get said?
        return norm(plan[move["q"]].question) in norm(text)
    return False                            # interrupted probe/clarify: didn't happen
  • Progress is event-sourced: probes used, questions asked and the current question are all computed from delivered moves, never from counters.
  • In the design, barge-in also invalidates the pending speculative moves, because the context they were drafted for has changed.

stages.name: Treat the answer as one answer
stages.claim: merge since the last heard move
stages.html:
One answer:last move heardcandidate turnbarge-incandidate turnall joined by answer_since(last_delivered_turn)
  • answer_since(last_delivered_turn) joins every candidate turn since the last move they heard.
  • The warm tier re-analyses the whole merged answer when each turn commits, and resets only when a reply was heard in full.
  • Without this, one answer split by a barge-in would be scored as two thin answers.

stages.name: Tell noise from interruption
stages.html:
Event Behaviour () Test
cough / tap, no words agent pauses, resumes within 2 s (false_interruption_timeout) V-21
"mm-hm" under 0.4 s ignored V-23
"Sorry, one second" audio stops within ~0.5 s, turn stored interrupted=1 V-20

Metric: false barge-in rate. Most conversational tuning assumes peers; an interviewer holds the floor longer.

followUps.question: What if the "interruption" was the agent's own voice through the speakers?
followUps.html:
Then it is echo, and the guard can only protect the record.

Control Protects
client-side AEC (primary) the conversation: no false interruption
the echo guard the record: barge-in fires on sound before any transcript exists

See Q35.

followUps.question: "Log the full response; the model generated it."
followUps.html:
The record must match what was said aloud.

Wrong:log the generated textcontext and scorer assume words the candidate never heard
Right:log the truncated textmarked interrupted

followUps.question: Should the interrupted LLM call be cancelled too?
🧪 The candidate interrupts after the planned question was fully said, during a trailing "take your time". Does the question count?
followUps.html:
Yes: they heard the question.

  • delivered checks that the planned question's text is inside what was spoken.
  • Only the tail was lost, so the plan advances.

followUps.question: Would you ever disable barge-in?
followUps.html:
For fixed lines where interruption would break something; never for questions.

Line Interruptions
the closing line after a time or budget stop off: the call is ending either way
questions always on: a candidate who can't interrupt can't ask for clarification

dontSay: "We detect interruptions from the transcript."
"The full response goes into history."

spine: Why echo is a scoring bug
Layer 1, cancel it in the browser
Layer 2, drop it before the record
real-time-systems-q35.testing: whether you see echo as a correctness problem in an interview product, and whether you know why a server-side check can protect the record but not the conversation.
real-time-systems-q35.trap: "WebRTC has echo cancellation, so it's handled." AEC misses, and a miss is silent.
real-time-systems-q35.spoken:
Beat Say
1 · Why echo is a scoring bug "Candidates use laptop speakers as often as headphones. If Rachel's voice leaks back into the mic, every downstream stage misreads it: turn detection thinks the candidate is talking, barge-in cuts Rachel off, STT transcribes her words as the candidate's, and the Assessor scores our own question as their answer. That last one is a scoring-validity bug, not an annoyance."
2 · Layer 1, cancel it in the browser "The primary control is the browser's acoustic echo cancellation, on in the capture settings with noise suppression and gain control. It is primary because only the browser has the far-end reference, the exact audio being played, so it can predict the echo and subtract it."
3 · Layer 2, drop it before the record "Behind it, a server-side echo guard. When a candidate turn ends while Rachel is speaking or within 1.5 seconds of her stopping, we compare its text with what Rachel just said. If at least 80 percent of the candidate's words appear, in order, in Rachel's text, and it is at least three words, we drop the turn before it is committed. It never reaches the brain, the transcript store or the Panel."
4 · What the guard can't do "The honest limit: the guard can't prevent an echo-triggered interruption. Barge-in fires on sound within about 150 milliseconds, and the transcript it needs arrives 200 to 300 later."
5 · The weak spots "The weak spots are partial leaks from laptop speakers in a hard-walled room, which verbatim matching won't catch, and a brief flash of the echo in the live caption."
Close "AEC protects the conversation; the guard protects the score."

stages.name: Why echo is a scoring bug
stages.html:
Stage What echo does
turn detection sees speech: "the candidate is talking"
barge-in fires: Rachel stops mid-word
STT transcribes Rachel's words as the candidate's
Assessor / Panel scores our question as their answer

stages.name: Layer 1, cancel it in the browser
stages.html:
AEC:far-end audio playedadaptive filter predicts its echo at the micsubtracts the predictionclean capture
  • getUserMedia with echoCancellation, noiseSuppression, autoGainControl, mono, through the LiveKit SDK.
  • AEC learns an adaptive filter for how the speaker output arrives back at the mic and subtracts the prediction; a double-talk detector freezes adaptation while both talk, so the candidate's voice isn't cancelled.
  • It needs 3–4 s to converge, so the most echo-prone moment is the opening line. The device check should play throwaway audio first so the filter converges before the first real question.

stages.name: Layer 2, drop it before the record
stages.claim: a string check, not a classifier
stages.html:
Prove it — the containment score the guard uses (run with Python 3):

import re
from difflib import SequenceMatcher
norm = lambda s: " ".join(re.findall(r"[a-z0-9']+", s.lower()))
def containment(user, agent):
    u, a = norm(user), norm(agent)
    m = SequenceMatcher(None, u, a, autojunk=False)
    return sum(b.size for b in m.get_matching_blocks()) / len(u)
agent = "Tell me about a backend system you designed and the trade-offs you made."
print(round(containment("a backend system you designed and the trade offs", agent), 2))  # → 1.0
print(round(containment("I designed a payments ledger on Postgres", agent), 2))           # → 0.42
  • Rule (): drop when containment ≥ 0.8, the turn ends while the agent speaks or within 1.5 s after, and it's ≥ 3 words. The drop is StopResponse in on_user_turn_completed, before the turn is committed.
  • Containment, not similarity: the leaked fragment is usually a part of the agent's sentence, so "how much of the user text is inside the agent text" is the right measure.

stages.name: What the guard can't do
stages.html:
t (ms) Event
0 Rachel's voice leaks into the mic
~150 barge-in fires on sound; Rachel stops
~350–450 the transcript exists; the guard says "that was us" and drops the turn

The candidate has already heard Rachel cut herself off. That's why AEC is primary and the guard is defence in depth.

stages.name: The weak spots
stages.html:
Weak spot Response
partial overlap from laptop speakers in a hard-walled room if echo_suppressed_total runs high, headphones become a hard gate
the live caption flashes the echo STT text streams to the browser before the turn ends
not built yet ducking agent audio during speech, headphone detection
  • A candidate on laptop speakers in a hard-walled room can leak partial overlap that verbatim containment won't catch. If echo_suppressed_total runs high, headphones become a hard gate ().
  • The live caption may flash the echo briefly, because STT text streams to the browser before the turn ends.
  • Other mitigations from the literature we don't have yet: ducking agent audio during speech and headphone detection.

followUps.question: Why not do AEC on the server?
followUps.html:
The server doesn't have the far-end reference as the speaker played it.

Needed Where it is
device delay, room acoustics, volume on the client
the playback signal local to the browser

followUps.question: 🧪 The candidate echoes part of the question back. Will the guard drop it?
followUps.html:
It depends on the overlap, and the rule can misfire.

Against the question above, run through the same function:

"So you want the trade-offs of the ledger design?"   → 0.6   kept
"the backend system I designed"                       → 0.93  dropped, if within 1.5 s
  • The second is a real answer opening that the guard would drop: the score is computed on characters and the candidate reused Rachel's words.
  • Limits: the time window and the 3-word floor; suppressed turns are reviewed by hand.
  • If false drops show up: compare on words, not characters, and raise the floor.

followUps.question: "Just require headphones."
followUps.html:
It is a fairness and access cost: some candidates don't have them.

Headphones When
recommended in the device check
mandatory only if measured echo rates demand it

followUps.question: Does Krisp noise cancellation help with echo?
followUps.html:
Partly; don't rely on it for this.

Krisp BVC
does keeps one primary speaker and masks background voices, so a faint leaked voice can be suppressed
is not an echo canceller: it has no far-end reference

followUps.question: How would you know if echo is hurting scores in production?
followUps.html:
Two counters and a join.

echo_suppressed_total and barge_in_total{source="suspected_echo"}, per sessionjoined with device type (speakers or headset)rate per cohort

A high rate in one cohort is a fairness finding, not only a UX one.

dontSay: "The guard prevents echo interruptions."
"WebRTC handles echo."

spine: Why a wrong term is unfair
real-time-systems-q36.testing: that you know a mangled term is a scoring error, not a cosmetic one, and that you fixed it with measurements rather than a word list you hoped would work.
real-time-systems-q36.trap: "we boost keywords" with no numbers and no limit. Boosting can't create a word that wasn't said, and the list has a cap.
real-time-systems-q36.spoken:
Beat Say
1 · Why a wrong term is unfair "A garbled technical term isn't a neutral error. If a candidate says 'idempotent' and the transcript says 'item potent', the Assessor sees someone who can't name the technology they claim to know. So vocabulary is a fairness problem."
2 · Listening: keyterm prompting "On the listening side we use Deepgram Nova-3's keyterm prompting: up to 100 terms per session, given to the model as context, which biases decoding toward those spellings when the audio is ambiguous."
3 · Which 100 terms "The list is built per interview in priority order: the plan's own terms first, then the topics in play, curated terms for the section, the candidate's stated stack, and a 66-term backend base list, because the cap cuts from the end."
4 · Speaking: the pronunciation lexicon "On the speaking side there is a versioned pronunciation lexicon: 23 entries, so Rachel says Kubernetes for k8s and E T C D for etcd. The transcript keeps the original text; only the spoken form changes."
5 · The last line of defence "The last line of defence is the LLM: the Reviewer and Panel are told the transcript comes from speech recognition, and they reconstruct 'item potency keys' as idempotency keys from context."
6 · What we measured "We measured it on a golden set. Keyterms took term recall from 79 to 83 percent up to 89 on US voices, and the production config reached 96 on the Indian-accent voice. The lexicon went from 88 to 100 percent on a round-trip test after one fix."
Close "Bias the listening, fix the speaking, and gate on term recall."

stages.html:
Heard Transcribed without keyterms Effect on scoring
idempotent "item potent" candidate looks vague
GraphQL "BRAFQL" claim unreadable
Raft "RAF" wrong technology
OOM killed "UAM killed" incident story garbled

( real errors from the golden set, 24 Sep 2026)

stages.name: Listening: keyterm prompting
stages.html:

real-time-systems-q37.testing: whether a decision that sounds exclusionary was measured, and whether you know exactly who pays for it.
real-time-systems-q37.trap: "most candidates speak English anyway." That's an assumption; the answer is a measurement and a named cost.
real-time-systems-q37.spoken:
Beat Say
1 · The decision "We run Deepgram in Indian English, en-IN, not the multilingual code-switching mode, and we decided it with numbers. The interview is conducted in English and says so up front; Hinglish is tolerated, not supported."
2 · The measurement that forced it "On the same golden set, multilingual mode did capture Hinglish, but technical-term recall fell from 86 percent to 76. In a technical interview, words like idempotent, etcd and GraphQL are the evidence. A mangled term makes a strong candidate look vague, which is its own unfairness. Multilingual mode also returns mixed Latin and Devanagari script, which breaks the English keyterm list, the scoring prompts and the verbatim evidence quotes a recruiter reads."
3 · What we rejected "So I rejected multilingual mode for everyone, and switching models per turn. The voice side agrees: the TTS vendor's Hindi voice is weak."
4 · What it cost "The cost is real and I'd say it first. On en-IN, Hinglish doesn't come back garbled, it comes back empty. The words silently vanish, which is worse than a bad transcript because nobody sees it. The mitigation, detect that VAD heard speech but the transcript is empty and ask the candidate to repeat in English, is designed, not built. Candidates who code-switch more pay this cost, so it belongs in the per-cohort fairness audit. And the numbers come from synthetic voices."
5 · What would reopen it "It reopens for a role whose working language is Hindi, or a multilingual model that closes the term-recall gap on the same golden set."
Close "Measured, stated to candidates, and its cost named."

en-IN + keyterms multi + keyterms

Keyterm list, scoring prompts, evidence quotes work disrupted

  • Hinglish on en-IN → empty transcript. A candidate who explains a key idea in Hindi loses that answer unless they repeat it.
  • Mitigation: VAD speech + empty transcript → Rachel asks them to repeat in English. Not built.
  • Code-switch category in the golden set: 50% (reported, not gated).

  • A role whose working language is Hindi.

followUps.html:
It has a fairness cost, and I'd rather own it than hide it.

A wrong transcript is visible; an empty one leaves no trace.

real-time-systems-q38.testing: whether you check the measurement before the system, and whether you can tell a small miss on a gate from a budget failure.
real-time-systems-q38.trap: switching TTS vendors over 19 ms without asking whether the number is right, or whether it's measured under the conditions that matter.
real-time-systems-q38.spoken:
Beat Say
1 · Trust the measurement first "First, trust the measurement. Our first TTS benchmark read 1.3 seconds, and the system was fine: the harness abandoned streams midway, which discarded the pooled connection, so every later measurement paid a cold connect. Once it drained every stream, warm p50 was 319 milliseconds. So I always suspect the harness first."
2 · Is 19 ms the real problem? "Second, is 19 milliseconds the problem? The 300 line is one slice of an 800 millisecond p95 budget, and 319 is warm p50 on a single stream. The real risk is what it becomes under concurrency and at p95, which we haven't measured. If it is 450 under load, the budget fails on arithmetic."
3 · What's already optimised "Third, what is already done: sentence chunking with a 12-word forced flush, one TTS stream per segment started immediately, and warm pooled connections. The flush alone cut first audio on a long unpunctuated sentence from 677 to 437 milliseconds."
4 · The options "The options, in order: try the vendor's nearest region, try a faster engine like Cartesia or ElevenLabs Flash or the design's Smallest.ai, or accept 320 and rebalance the budget."
5 · The decision rule "The rule: decide on p95 under target concurrency, not on warm p50 of one stream."
Close "Check the harness, read the miss against the budget, then decide under load."

after drains every stream to the end 319 ms warm p50

A measurement bug, not a system change ( 24 Sep 2026).

Prove it — what the number does to N1 ( budget):

p95 budget with TTS at 300    690 ms
TTS at 319                     709 ms   still under 800
TTS at 450 under load          840 ms   fails N1 on arithmetic
  • The gate says FAIL; the budget says fine at one stream. What's unmeasured is p95 at 500–1000 concurrent streams.

Technique Measured effect

fallback voice (OpenAI TTS) after one retry availability, not speed

stages.html:

  • Keep the golden harness in the loop for any vendor change: TTFB, lexicon round trip and MOS-style listening checks.

followUps.html:
One stream per reply holds the first byte back for the whole generation.

Per reply Per segment
Flush sent only when the whole reply ends (LiveKit's Deepgram TTS) at each segment
Segment 1 waits synthesises while segment 2 is generated

Pooled connections make per-segment streams cheap, and LiveKit deprecated multiple segments per stream.

followUps.question: 🧪 What does the chunker do with a 25-word question and one full stop at the end?
followUps.html:
Two forced flushes, then a one-word tail.

Segment Words
1 12
2 12
3 the final word with the full stop

A one-word tail is fine for latency but can sound clipped: one reason to prefer punctuation in generated text.

followUps.question: "Warm p50 is what users experience."
followUps.html:
Users experience p95, on the first turn too.

  • And under whatever concurrency the vendor is serving.
  • Warm p50 of a single stream is the most flattering number available.

followUps.question: Who owns this decision?
followUps.html:
The budget owner: it is a product decision with a cost line.

I'd bring

TTS is 55% of the turn budget.

real-time-systems-q39.testing: whether you know that multi-agent in a voice loop is a scheduling problem first: who is allowed on the clock, and what happens when an agent isn't ready.
real-time-systems-q39.trap: a supervisor that fans out to five agents on every turn and waits for them.
real-time-systems-q39.spoken:
Beat Say
1 · Why the naive design fails "The naive design puts a supervisor in the turn: the candidate stops, the supervisor fans out to five agents, reconciles, generates, then speaks. That is three to six seconds. Human tolerance for silence is about 800 milliseconds, so it is unshippable."
2 · Split by latency tier "So the agents are partitioned by latency budget, not by function."
3 · T0, the turn "T0 is the turn itself, under 800 milliseconds: an intent guard, which is regexes, then Chair, which is rules and picks the next move in about a millisecond, then the speaker, Chanakya, which says it, or a canned redirect line if the candidate went off topic. Only the speaker and the redirect ever produce audio."
4 · T1, while they speak "T1 runs while the candidate is still talking, 2 to 20 seconds: on each final STT phrase, debounced 300 milliseconds, the Assessor scores the answer so far, the Prober decides whether there is a gap worth probing and suggests a hint, and Sentinel checks integrity with rules. They fan out in parallel and write into a per-interview context. Chair reads that at the end of the turn if it is ready; if not, it uses a word-count fallback. The candidate never waits on T1."
5 · T2, after the call "T2 runs after the call: two Panel assessors with different framings and no shared context, a Reconciler, a Registrar that writes the scorecard, and in parallel a Reviewer that writes per-question feedback. The branches share no state."
6 · The seam with LiveKit "The seam with LiveKit is clean: LiveKit owns the audio loop, VAD, turn detection and interruption; the LangGraph graph sits in the slot where a LiveKit agent would normally call an LLM, and is run once per turn."
7 · The invariants "And a few invariants keep it working: Chair selects and never generates, every write is keyed by turn, and the planned question is spoken verbatim."
Close "Multi-agent in a voice loop is scheduling first: who is allowed on the clock."

stages.html:
candidate stops → supervisor → fan out to 5 agents → reconcile → generate → TTS
                  └──────────────── 3–6 s ────────────────┘   vs  ~800 ms tolerance

stages.name: Split by latency tier
stages.html: Stadiums contain LLM calls; rectangles are rules or code.

stages.html:
Node Kind Does

stages.html:
T1:final STT phrasedebounce 300 msAssessor ∥ Prober ∥ Sentinelinsights[turn]Chair reads it if ready
  • Assessor scores 1–5 with evidence; never decides what to ask.
  • Prober returns needs_probe + a hint; never scores.
  • Sentinel returns flags (rules); diarization adds a second_voice_signal, a signal, never a verdict.
  • Writes go to InterviewContext.insights[turn], not graph state, to avoid checkpoint races with the turn's own run.
  • Its own budget (calls, tokens) and circuit breakers: when it runs out, T1 stops and Chair falls back.

  • Panel: assessor A (strict reading) ∥ assessor B (evidence first) → Reconciler resolves gaps over one point toward stronger verbatim evidence → Registrar persists.
  • Reviewer: per planned question, expected / said / did well / missed / model answer.
  • asyncio.gather: one failing never blocks the other; the Reviewer never reads the Panel.

Concern Owner

brain = LLMAdapter(graph, config=config, context=ictx, stream_mode="custom")

stages.name: The invariants
stages.claim: six rules that keep it working
stages.html:
# Invariant Keeps
1 Chair selects, never generates the turn inside its budget
2 only the speaker and redirect speak internal calls out of the audio
3 every graph write is keyed by turn and overwrites preemptive re-runs idempotent
4 T1 writes to context, not graph state no checkpoint races with the turn's run

6 T2 branches are independent one failure from blocking the other

followUps.question: Why is T1 allowed to be slow?
followUps.html:
Because nothing waits for it.

T1 for this answer Chair uses
ready the insight
not ready a heuristic: a short first answer gets one probe

A slow T1 makes the interview less adaptive, never slower.

followUps.question: "Multi-agent means the agents talk to each other."
followUps.html:
Not here: they communicate through shared, typed state.

T1 writes insightsInterviewContextChair reads them

No agent calls another, and no conversation between agents happens in the turn.

followUps.question: Why run T0 and T1 in the same process?
followUps.html:
They share a session, state and lifecycle; splitting adds a network hop to every read.

Layout Cost
v0.1: pending moves through Redis ~140 ms per turn
co-located event-loop discipline (Q48)

followUps.question: 🧪 T1 finishes 50 ms after Chair already ran. What happens to the insight?
followUps.html:
It is stored for the record but doesn't affect this turn's move.

  • Persisted on the committed answer.
  • If the candidate keeps talking after the reply, the answer is re-analysed as one merged answer, and the next Chair run can use it.

followUps.question: How would you add a new agent?
followUps.html:
Ask which tier it belongs to first.

It needs Then it is
the turn rules, or pre-computed
to run during speech a T1 branch writing to context under a deadline
the full transcript T2

Then add it to the call-case suite, so its effect on the conversation is tested.

dontSay: "A supervisor agent orchestrates everything each turn."
That the Assessor's T1 score is the final score.

real-time-systems-q40.testing: whether you put the model where judgement is needed and code where guarantees are needed, and can say which is which.
real-time-systems-q40.trap: "an LLM supervisor is more flexible." Flexibility in the component that enforces the budget, the plan and the probe limits is exactly what you don't want.
real-time-systems-q40.spoken:
Beat Say
1 · The decision "Chair decides what happens next: greet, ask the next planned question, probe, clarify, redirect, wrap up, or pause. It is plain Python rules evaluated in order, first match wins, and it runs in about a millisecond. It never writes question text."
2 · The constraint "Three reasons. Latency: Chair is on the clock every turn, and an LLM call there costs more than the whole budget. Guarantees: Chair enforces the things that must always hold: at most two probes per question, at most two clarifications, stop following up after twenty minutes so every planned question gets asked, wrap at the turn limit, and never count a move the candidate didn't actually hear. Those are invariants, and I want them in code with 27 unit tests, not in a prompt. And auditability: every decision is logged with its reason, so a human can see why the interview went where it went."
3 · What we rejected "So an LLM supervisor was rejected. The judgement lives around Chair, not in it. The Prober, an LLM, decides whether an answer has a gap worth probing and what it is. The speaker phrases it. Chair just combines those signals with the plan and the limits."
4 · What it cost "The cost is rigidity: new behaviours mean new rules, and the rule order is itself a design decision that has to be tested."
5 · What would reopen it "What would reopen it is a behaviour the rules can't express that the evals show matters."
Close "Models where judgement is needed, code where guarantees are needed."

Order If Move
1 turn 0 greet
2 pause or end pause or wrap
3 clarify, under 2 clarify
4 off-topic, under 2 redirect
5 don't know, or intro done next question
6 probe budget spent, or past 20 min next question

8 insight not ready, no probe yet, answer under 60 words probe

stages.name: The constraint
stages.html:
Prove it — the limits Chair enforces ( hot_path.py):

MAX_CLARIFIES_PER_Q = 2          # "repeat that?" forever would be an LLM call each time
MAX_REDIRECTS_PER_Q = 2          # an off-topic candidate can't stall the plan
MAX_TURNS           = 80         # at the limit Rachel wraps; the Panel still runs
FOLLOW_UP_CUTOFF_S  = 20 * 60    # after this, remaining planned questions come first
max_probes          per question from the plan (e.g. 2, 1, 1)
  • Progress is a fold over delivered moves: probes used and the current question are computed from what the candidate heard, never from counters (Q34).
  • Every decision logs: CHAIR turn=N intent=… → probe q=0 (prober: …) [0.4ms, insight=ready].

stages.claim: an LLM supervisor, in two forms
stages.html:
Option Why not
LLM supervisor picks the move a model call on the clock; limits become suggestions; decisions hard to reproduce
LLM with the limits written in its prompt the model can still violate them, and a test can't prove it won't
a learned policy no training data yet; needs the scoring reference set that doesn't exist

stages.name: What it cost
stages.html:
Cost Example
new behaviour = a new rule and a new test —
rule order matters "clarify" before "don't know"; "pause" before "end", so "can we finish this later?" pauses
a crude fallback heuristic a short answer gets one probe; only matters when T1 is late

  • New behaviour = new rule + new test. The order matters: "clarify" is checked before "don't know", "pause" before "end" (so "can we finish this later?" pauses instead of ending).
  • The fallback heuristic (a short answer gets one probe) is crude; it only matters when T1 is late.
  • In the full design, Chair also selects among speculative moves with staleness and confidence checks; that part isn't built.

stages.html:
Evidence Likely fix
the interview repeatedly probed the wrong thing, or moved on too early, in ways a rule can't express a better signal into Chair (a smarter Prober), not an LLM in Chair
  • Reviewer or human feedback showing the interview repeatedly probed the wrong thing, or moved on too early, in ways a rule can't express.
  • Even then, the likely fix is a better signal into Chair (a smarter Prober), not an LLM in Chair.

followUps.html:
As a pure function of state.

Level Checks
27 unit tests over state fixtures given these delivered moves, this intent and this insight, the move must be X
the live call suite (V-02 to V-05) the same rules, end to end

followUps.html:
Chair has about a dozen rules, because it only decides the kind of move.

Part Owner
what must be guaranteed rules
is this answer vague, what is the gap, how to phrase it LLM agents

followUps.html:
The budget rule fires first.

needs_probe, 2 of 2 probes used ─▶ next question, reason "probe budget spent (2/2)"

The Prober's opinion is input, not authority.

followUps.question: Where does adaptivity come from, then?
followUps.html:
From the signals Chair reads, and in the design from a coverage ledger.

next target = highest  weight × (1 − confidence)

That steering algorithm is still a docstring in the design, and I'd say so.

That rules are "less intelligent" without saying what they guarantee.

real-time-systems-q41.testing: whether an LLM agent in a real-time loop has a structured output, a trigger, a deadline and a fallback, or just "runs".
real-time-systems-q41.trap: "the Prober generates the follow-up question." It produces a hint; Chair decides; the speaker phrases.
real-time-systems-q41.spoken:
Beat Say
1 · What the Prober is for "The Prober is the agent that makes the interview adaptive. It reads the question and the answer so far and returns two things: whether the answer needs a probe, and a hint under 15 words naming the single most useful gap. It doesn't score; that is the Assessor's job, deliberately separate."
2 · What it looks for "It looks for answers that are vague, generic, memorised-sounding, or claims without specifics: no numbers, no decisions, no sense of the candidate's own role."
3 · When it runs "It runs while the candidate is still talking. Deepgram finalises phrases before the end of the turn is decided, so on each final phrase we restart the analysis of the whole answer so far, debounced by 300 milliseconds. By the time the candidate stops, the insight for this answer is usually ready."
4 · How Chair uses it "Chair then decides. If there is probe budget left for this question and the Prober says there is a gap, Chair picks a probe and passes the hint to the speaker, which asks one follow-up about something specific they said. If the Prober says no gap, Chair moves on."
5 · When it's late "If it isn't ready in time, Chair doesn't wait. It falls back to a heuristic: if no probe has been used on this question and the answer was under 60 words, probe once on a concrete detail; otherwise move on."
6 · What it doesn't do "It never writes the question, never picks the move, and never blocks the turn."
Close "A structured output, a trigger, a deadline and a fallback."

stages.name: What the Prober is for
stages.html:
Agent Does Never
Assessor scores decides what to ask
Prober finds gaps scores
  • The Assessor scores but never decides what to ask. The Prober finds gaps but never scores. A model that generated a question is measurably more generous to answers matching its shape, so the roles stay apart.

stages.name: What it looks for
stages.claim: a verdict and a short hint
stages.html:
Prove it — the output contract ( background.py):

class _Probe(BaseModel):
    needs_probe: bool   # vague, generic, unsupported or shallow?
    probe_hint: str     # the specific gap, under 15 words; empty if none
  • Prompt asks: vague, generic, memorised-sounding, or claimed without specifics (numbers, decisions, their own role)? Name the single most useful gap.
  • The transcript is labelled as speech and possibly partial.

t Event

+300 ms debounce elapses → T1 starts on the whole answer so far
new phrase previous T1 task cancelled, restarted on the longer answer

Answers under 4 words skip T1; the analysis targets the question the candidate actually heard.

real-time-systems-q42.testing: whether you separate what must be decided this turn from what can be flagged for a human, and whether you'd let a detector accuse a candidate.
real-time-systems-q42.trap: an LLM classifier on every turn for intent, or auto-ending an interview on a detected "integrity" issue.
real-time-systems-q42.spoken:
Beat Say
1 · Two layers, two budgets "Two layers with different budgets. Intent has to be decided on the clock, every turn, because it changes what Rachel says next. Behaviour, meaning integrity signals, doesn't; it can be flagged for a human afterwards."
2 · Intent on the clock "For intent, the intent guard is a set of regexes, not an LLM. It classifies the candidate's last utterance into answer, clarify, don't know, off-topic, pause or end. The order matters: pause is checked before end, so 'can I finish this later' saves their place instead of ending. Some rules have length limits: off-topic only fires on short utterances, so a long answer that mentions a movie isn't redirected. Chair then acts: clarify rephrases the question, don't know moves on, off-topic gets a canned redirect, pause saves and closes resumably."
3 · Behaviour off the clock "For behaviour, Sentinel runs in the warm tier. Today it flags known prompt-injection patterns, and diarization adds a second-voice signal when more than one speaker label appears in an answer. Both are stored as flags for review."
4 · Signals, never verdicts "Nothing is auto-rejected and nothing is said to the candidate mid-interview: a false accusation there is severe and unrecoverable. And the injection defence isn't the flag. It is that the decision path is code: Chair decides which question comes next, so injection can change how something is worded, never whether a question is skipped or the interview ends."
5 · What's weak "What is weak: regexes miss paraphrases, and the second-voice signal has never been tested on a real two-speaker recording."
Close "Decide intent on the clock with rules; flag behaviour for a human."

It would put a model call on the clock for a decision five patterns mostly cover.

followUps.html:

auto-end an innocent candidate accused on a false positive, live, with no way to take it back

the 14-word hedge with a real number answer: it matches "don't know" but is over the 12-word limit
"no idea" dont_know

A hedge inside a real answer isn't "I have no experience here".

followUps.html:
Per class, weighted by consequence.

Step Detail
label a sample of real candidate turns with the true intent
measure precision and recall per class
weight a false "end" or "pause" is far worse than a missed "clarify"

The weighting decides whether a rule stays.

real-time-systems-q43.testing: whether you understand evaluator independence as a structural property, and whether your scoring claims are backed by a measurement or just by the architecture diagram.
real-time-systems-q43.trap: "we use multiple agents, so the score is more accurate." Independence and a reference set make it more accurate; more agents alone just cost more.
real-time-systems-q43.spoken:
Beat Say
1 · The decision "Two separations. First, the component that asks is never the component that scores. During the call the Assessor scores each answer and the Prober finds gaps, but Chair picks the move and the speaker phrases it. Second, the in-call score only steers; it is provisional and never shown. The score of record comes after the call, from a Panel: two assessors read the full transcript independently, then a Reconciler resolves differences over one point in favour of the stronger verbatim evidence, and a Registrar writes the scorecard. Every score has to cite quotes from the transcript."
2 · The constraint "The constraint is bias, latency and durability. A model that generated a question tends to be more generous to answers that fit the shape it expected. Independent assessors with long context and strong models take seconds. And in the design the Panel sits behind a queue, so a crashed worker retries instead of losing the scorecard of an interview that can't be re-run."
3 · What we rejected "So I rejected the interviewer scoring, judges in sequence, and a live score of record."
4 · What it cost "The honest weakness: the claim that consensus improves quality isn't measured yet. Our answer-level Scorer's first golden run, against provisional labels, had a mean error of 1.02 on a 0 to 10 scale with only 54 percent within one point: it scores generously. Repeatability was excellent and all 12 bias traps passed."
5 · What would reopen it "It reopens if two independent assessors agree no better than one assessor run twice."
Close "Consistent, but not yet calibrated, and I say so."

When Scores Picks the question Output
T1, during speech Assessor (1–5 + evidence) — provisional, steers Chair
T0, the turn — Chair (rules) the move
T2, after the call Panel A (strict) ∥ Panel B (evidence first) → Reconciler — scorecard of record (0–5 per competency + readiness)
T2 Scorer (0–10 per answer from anchored criteria) — per-question numbers

Confirmation bias the question generator favours answers shaped like its expectation.
Latency coupling fusing scoring into the fast path forces the worse of both budgets.
N7 durability a scoring job inline in a pod that dies loses the scorecard. A queue makes it retryable, keyed on (session_id, rubric_version, prompt_version) so a duplicate delivery overwrites instead of appending. The prototype still scores in the job's shutdown hook, which is exactly that risk.

judges in sequence, each seeing the last collapses to one opinion with extra token cost

stages.html:
Prove it — first scoring golden run ( 26 Sep 2026, 52 answers × 3 runs, labels provisional):

Check Result Target

within ±1 54% ≥ 80%

  • The model scores about a point high across every answer kind; the worst is long wrong answers (labels 0.8, model 3.0).
  • The labels are an LLM's first pass awaiting human review, so the run is provisional.
  • The Panel's reconciliation rule is a prompt, not an algorithm, and has no disagreement baseline yet.

stages.html:
Evidence Then
target human-labelled transcripts, ≥ 0.8 agreement between assessors, ≥ 95% on re-runs (N4)

  • Target: a reference set of human-labelled transcripts with ≥ 0.8 agreement between assessors, and ≥ 95% agreement on re-runs (N4).
  • If two independent assessors agree no better than one assessor run twice, the Panel is cost without value, and I'd drop to one strong assessor plus human review of low-confidence scores.

followUps.question: "Two LLM judges are just two samples of the same model."
followUps.html:
Partly true: same model, correlated errors.

Independence comes from
separate calls no shared context
different framings strict reading against evidence first
design a third, counterfactual framing: what would disqualify this candidate?

Whether that decorrelates enough is what the reference set has to show.

followUps.question: What do you show when the assessors disagree?
followUps.html:
The disagreement itself, on the scorecard **.**

  • panel_agreement and a dissent note.
  • Disagreement means the transcript underdetermines the score, which is when a human should look.

followUps.question: 🧪 An answer is mangled by speech recognition but correct. What should the scorer do, and does it?
followUps.html:
Score it within 1.5 points of its clean twin; on the first run it did.

ASR-mangled Clean twin

All three passed ( bias trap in the golden set).

the transcript is data, not instructions and Sentinel flags the attempt

That the in-call score is shown to anyone.

real-time-systems-q44.testing: whether you designed the feedback output as a structured contract, and whether you know where an LLM can compensate for an upstream error and where it can't.
real-time-systems-q44.trap: "the LLM fixes the transcript." It fixes the analysis; the record still holds the slip.
real-time-systems-q44.spoken:
Beat Say
1 · What it's for "The Panel produces the score; the Reviewer produces the study material."
2 · What it returns "After every mock interview or revision session, it goes through each planned question that was actually asked and returns a structured review: three to six points a standard answer at the candidate's level would cover, what they actually said, what they did well, left empty rather than invented, what they missed, and a model answer in headed sections ending with how to frame it. On revision sessions it also gives the topic a 1 to 5 rating that moves it up or down a revision ladder."
3 · Reading past ASR slips "Speech recognition mistakes: its prompt says the transcript comes from ASR, and to ignore accent, grammar and filler and judge content. A language model has seen idempotency keys in context thousands of times, so it reconstructs the intended term. In a live test the transcript said 'item potency keys' and the Reviewer's did-well column said 'mentioned idempotency keys for safe retries'."
4 · Independent of the Panel "It runs in parallel with the Panel and never reads its output, so a failure in one never blocks the other, and the feedback isn't anchored on the score."
5 · Its limits "The limit: it fixes the analysis, not the record. The stored quote still shows the slip."
Close "Structured feedback, independent of the score, and honest about what it can't rebuild."

Panel Reviewer
Output scorecard of record, per competency per-question study material
Reads transcript + rubric transcript + plan + candidate profile
Model tier judge judge
Revision sessions — 1–5 rating → topic ladder

stages.html:

class ReviewItem(BaseModel):
    question_index: int
    expected: list[str]         # 3–6 points a standard answer at their level covers
    said: list[str]             # faithful paraphrase; empty if they didn't answer
    did_well: list[str]         # specific, not praise; may be empty

  • Follow-ups actually asked are attached to their question, so the review sees the probes too.

Transcript Reviewer's reading

  • It can't rebuild what was never transcribed: a Hinglish sentence that came back empty, or a turn split at a pause, is simply missing.

  • asyncio.gather of Panel, Reviewer and Scorer: one failing never blocks the others.

  • The evidence quotes on the scorecard still show "item potency". A recruiter reading them sees the error.
  • Reconstruction can be wrong in the other direction: generously reading a term the candidate didn't actually know. Labelled test cases in the scoring goldens cover "ASR-mangled" answers for that reason.

When Why
during the call the Prober reads the raw transcript live and probes "vague" answers
afterwards reconstruction only works when context is strong

Fixing vocabulary at the source is still the first lever.

By pitching it at their level, against what they said and missed.

Check Means How

real-time-systems-q45.testing: whether "gateway" means something precise in your system, and whether you kept business APIs, the media path and model routing apart.
real-time-systems-q45.trap: one gateway box that everything goes through, including the live audio and every model call.
real-time-systems-q45.spoken:
Beat Say
1 · The decision "There are three things people call a gateway in this system, and I keep them apart. The business gateway is a Spring Boot GraphQL service: roles, rubrics, interview sessions and scorecards, tenant-scoped on every resolver. Its startInterview mutation calls the control plane to provision a room. The control plane is FastAPI: it mints LiveKit tokens with the agent dispatch, creates rooms, handles webhooks idempotently and runs retention. The LLM gateway is a LiteLLM router, in-process inside each interview's job process, not a service. It routes model calls across providers, Groq dedicated, then shared, then Cerebras or Gemini, behind per-provider circuit breakers."
2 · The constraint "The constraint: no hop in the turn, and no business logic near the media. The media path is client, LiveKit SFU, agent. No gateway touches it."
3 · What we rejected "There is deliberately no gateway service to scale for model calls: a separate hop would add latency to every call, and its capacity would have to track the worker fleet anyway."
4 · What it cost "The cost is breaker state per process, and two front doors that could overlap."
5 · What would reopen it "It reopens if per-tenant model policy or spend caps must be enforced centrally."
Close "Three gateways, three jobs, and none of them in the media path."

  • The gateway scales on business requests; the agents scale on concurrent interviews. Different axes.
  • Scorecards must surface panel_agreement and a dissent note, and there's no auto-reject field: the decision is a human's.

real-time-systems-q46.testing: whether each dependency has a detection, a fallback and a candidate-visible behaviour, and whether you protect the one thing that can't be re-run.
real-time-systems-q46.trap: retries with backoff on every call. Against a dead vendor that's a timeout per turn, which is dead air.
real-time-systems-q46.spoken:
Beat Say
1 · The rule "The rule is that the candidate never hears silence, and a completed interview always produces a scorecard."
2 · Fail fast "First, fail fast. Every vendor call sits behind a circuit breaker per dependency: after five consecutive upstream failures, timeouts, 429s, 5xx, it opens, and every call fails immediately for a cooldown, then one trial call; a failure doubles the cooldown. So a dead vendor costs one detection, not a timeout on every turn."
3 · Per vendor, the ladder "Then per vendor. TTS: retry once, then switch to the secondary voice, and log the switch. The LLM for analysis: if the warm tier's provider is down, the warm tier just stops and Chair uses its fallback rule, so the interview gets less adaptive, not slower. STT: if confidence collapses, Rachel asks the candidate to repeat, and if it persists, offers text fallback."
4 · The floor "The floor: if all analysis is gone, the interview completes in scripted mode, the static plan with no adaptation. And if audio fails entirely, the candidate finishes by typing; the scorecard records the modality."
5 · Make sure the scorecard survives "Last, the scorecard: in the design the Panel sits behind a queue with a dead-letter table swept by a cron, so an interview that finished is never dropped."
Close "Fail fast, degrade by a ladder, and protect the scorecard."

stages.claim: never silence, never lose the scorecard
stages.html:

stages.name: Fail fast
stages.html:
Prove it — the state machine (run with Python 3; threshold 5, cooldown 20 s, doubles on a failed trial, capped at 300 s):

class Breaker:
    def __init__(self, threshold=5, cooldown=20.0):
        self.fails, self.threshold, self.cooldown, self.opened_at = 0, threshold, cooldown, None
    def state(self, now):
        if self.opened_at is None: return "CLOSED"
        return "HALF_OPEN" if now - self.opened_at >= self.cooldown else "OPEN"
    def record(self, ok, now):
        if ok: self.fails, self.opened_at = 0, None
        else:
            self.fails += 1
            if self.fails >= self.threshold or self.state(now) == "HALF_OPEN":
                self.opened_at, self.cooldown = now, min(self.cooldown * (2 if self.opened_at else 1), 300)
b = Breaker()
for t in range(5): b.record(False, t)
print(b.state(5), b.state(24), b.state(25))   # → OPEN HALF_OPEN HALF_OPEN
b.record(False, 25); print(b.state(26), b.cooldown)   # → OPEN 40.0
  • Only upstream faults count (connection errors, timeouts, 429, 5xx). A malformed structured reply is our bug and doesn't trip it.
  • One breaker per dependency: openai-speaker, openai-analyst, openai-judge, embeddings, Postgres.

stages.name: The floor
stages.html:
Floor Why it always exists
scripted mode every session is seeded with a complete static plan
text fallback the transcript is valid, the rubric unchanged; the scorecard records modality = text_fallback
  • Every session is seeded with a complete static plan so scripted mode always exists. Quality drops; the interview doesn't fail.
  • Text fallback: the transcript is valid, the rubric unchanged, the Panel consumes text either way; the scorecard records modality = text_fallback so a human can weigh it.

stages.html:
Scorecard: interview.completed to SQSon enqueue failure, retry with backoffpending_panel tableswept by a CronJob
  • interview.completed to SQS; on enqueue failure, retry with backoff, then write to a pending_panel table a CronJob sweeps. Idempotent on (session_id, rubric_version, prompt_version).

followUps.question: Why is the breaker state per process and not shared?
followUps.html:
Simplicity: no coordination service in the path.

1000 processes × 5 failures to open   =   up to 5000 failed calls, all fast-failing

If that load matters, a shared health signal can pre-open breakers.

followUps.question: "Just retry with exponential backoff."
followUps.html:
Retries are for transient blips; the breaker is for outages.

Against a dead vendor Per call
retry with backoff a full timeout on every turn, and more load on a struggling dependency
breaker an immediate failure into the fallback

followUps.question: 🧪 The TTS vendor recovers after 30 s. When does the primary voice come back?
followUps.html:
In the prototype, after a recovery check; in production I'd keep the secondary to the end of the session.

Behaviour
prototype LiveKit's fallback adapter marks the primary available again and moves back; both switches logged
design the voice is fixed per session

Two voice changes in one interview is worse than one: a gap between the design and the prototype.

followUps.question: How do you test this before a real outage?
followUps.html:
Fault injection per dependency, in a staging call.

kill the TTS keythrottle the LLMdrop Postgresrun the call-case suite

Each row of the ladder becomes a test with an expected candidate-visible behaviour.

dontSay: "We retry until it works."
That STT failover mid-stream is seamless (the stream must reconnect, and words in flight can be lost).

real-time-systems-q47.testing: whether you know a voice platform's ceiling is external concurrency and cost, not your cluster, and whether your numbers come with their assumptions.
real-time-systems-q47.trap: starting with node math. A cluster that can host 1000 interviews is useless if the TTS vendor serialises at 200 streams.
real-time-systems-q47.spoken:
Beat Say
1 · Vendors first "I'd start with the vendors, not the nodes. At 1000 concurrent interviews we hold 1000 simultaneous streams each to STT, to TTS and to the LLM provider. Those need committed concurrency quotas, and TTS first byte has to be verified at that concurrency, because it is 55 percent of the turn budget and we have only measured it on one warm stream. If that fails, nothing else matters."
2 · Four tiers, four scaling axes "Then four tiers, each scaling on its own axis. The FastAPI control plane is stateless and off the media path; three to six replicas cover it. The LiveKit SFU carries 2000 audio tracks, about 80 megabits, which is trivial bandwidth, but one node isn't comfortable at that track count, so it goes multi-node with Redis coordinating rooms, on-demand nodes in one Indian region."
3 · The numbers "The agents tier is the heavy one: one process per interview, so 1000 processes; at the planning assumption of half a vCPU and half a gigabyte each, that is about 125 pods of eight and 42 sixteen-core nodes at minimum, around 55 with autoscaling headroom. And the cold path, post-call scoring, scales on queue depth on spot nodes, around 134 workers to clear a batch of 1000 in half an hour."
4 · What breaks in order "What breaks, in order: vendor concurrency and cost first, SFU topology second, event-loop lag inside a job third, node CPU last."
5 · Setup order "So the setup order is contracts before clusters: vendor capacity first, then the SFU, the control plane, the agents fleet and the cold path."
6 · What's unproven "Every node number hangs off one assumption, interviews per pod, which is unmeasured, so the first thing I'd do is load-test it."
Close "The ceiling is vendor concurrency, not the cluster."

stages.name: Vendors first
stages.html:
Vendor 1000 concurrent Risk
STT (Deepgram, streaming) 1000 connections committed concurrency quota
TTS (streaming) 1000 connections first byte under load unmeasured; 55% of the budget
LLM (Groq, T1) 1000+ streams dedicated capacity; speculation is 2–3× tokens

Each vendor call behind a circuit breaker, so a throttled provider fails fast into the fallback ladder instead of burning a timeout × 1000.

stages.name: Four tiers, four scaling axes
stages.html:
Tier Scales on Nodes Note

LiveKit SFU tracks, connections on-demand, never spot multi-node + Redis at 2000 tracks

Cold path (panel workers) queue depth (KEDA, scale to zero) spot fills after interviews end

A spot eviction mid-interview is unrecoverable.

  • The candidate has left, and the interview can't be re-run.
  • The rule came from an earlier incident with the coturn relay: anything holding live media state runs on on-demand nodes, enforced by node selector in the chart.

followUps.html:

Quantity Driver
vendor-minutes STT, TTS

real-time-systems-q48.testing: whether you know that async code fails silently under a blocking call, and what you did structurally rather than by convention.
real-time-systems-q48.trap: "we use async, so nothing blocks." One sync SDK call blocks the whole loop.
real-time-systems-q48.spoken:
Beat Say
1 · The failure mode "The failure mode is event-loop starvation. Turn-taking is soft real time on an asyncio loop. Any accidentally blocking call, a sync SDK, parsing a big JSON response, a regex over a 45-minute transcript, a cold TLS handshake, stalls turn-taking, and the symptom isn't an error, it is dead air on a live call."
2 · Isolation by process "The structural fix is one process per interview. LiveKit Agents runs each job in its own subprocess, so a blocking call or a crash is contained to one conversation. That retired the design's old limit of 50 interviews per pod on a shared loop."
3 · Discipline inside the process "Inside the process the rules still apply, because the turn loop and the analysis share it: every analysis task has a deadline and is cancellable, CPU work goes off the loop, database writes run as background tasks or in threads, connections are warm before the first turn, and VAD is loaded before the job arrives."
4 · Budgets per run "There is also a budget per run. Each interview has a cap on model calls and tokens; when it is hit, a watchdog ends the call with a fixed closing line and still runs the evaluation. The analysis tier has its own smaller budget, so it can't starve the conversation."
5 · The metric that watches it "What watches it is event-loop lag per process, alerting at 50 milliseconds. The honest caveat: the in-process rules are disciplines, not guarantees, and the lag metric is designed, not shipped."
Close "Isolate by process, keep discipline inside it, and measure the lag."

stages.name: The failure mode
stages.html:
Culprit Where it hides
sync SDK call a new dependency someone added
json.loads on a large payload model or vendor responses
regex over the full transcript integrity checks
sync tokenizer for context trimming memory compaction
cold TLS handshake first call to a vendor

stages.name: Isolation by process
stages.claim: the blast radius is one interview
stages.html:
Isolation:workerone subprocess per joba blocking call or a crash hits one conversation
  • LiveKit Agents: worker → one subprocess per job. #processes = #concurrent interviews.
  • A blocking call or a crash hits one conversation; lag becomes a per-conversation metric.
  • Not a reason we chose LiveKit, but the biggest unplanned win of that choice.

stages.name: Discipline inside the process
stages.html:
Prove it — the patterns in the prototype (, abridged):

proc.userdata["vad"] = silero.VAD.load()            # prewarm: before any job arrives
_bg(db.add_turn(...))                                # DB writes as tasks, references kept
prof = await asyncio.to_thread(db.candidate_profile, cid)   # sync I/O in a thread
self.task.cancel(); self.task = asyncio.create_task(...)    # one in-flight T1 per answer

The design adds hard deadlines per T1 agent under a TaskGroup (e.g. 1800 ms, 900 ms); a missed deadline is a cancellation that the fallback ladder absorbs.

stages.name: Budgets per run
stages.html:
Budget Scope When exceeded
interview every model call in the job watchdog → fixed closing line (no model) → evaluation still runs
T1 background analysis only T1 stops; Chair uses its fallback
evaluation post-call scoring, isolated an interview that hit its limit still gets feedback

Budgets live in a context variable, so tasks and graph nodes started inside inherit them; nested budgets both count.

stages.name: The metric that watches it
stages.html:
Designed Detail
metric event_loop_lag_ms, alert on p99 > 50 ms
on sustained lag shed T1 work: the Assessor first, because it is provisional
escape hatch T0 and T1 on two event loops in one process: shared memory, no network hop
  • event_loop_lag_ms, alert p99 > 50 ms; on sustained lag, shed T1 work (drop the Assessor first; it's provisional).
  • Escape hatch if lag is hard to control: T0 and T1 on two event loops in one process (T0 on its own thread): shared memory, no network hop, scheduling isolation.

followUps.html:
Async means it won't wait on I/O you awaited.

Call inside a coroutine Effect on the loop
awaited I/O other coroutines run
any sync call holds the loop until it returns; every other coroutine waits

followUps.html:
Three instruments.

Instrument Shows
asyncio debug mode in staging slow-callback warnings
loop-lag metrics per process which conversation
per-turn latency traces a turn whose stages sum to far less than its total: time spent with the loop blocked

followUps.html:
It would add a network hop to every read Chair makes, and split state that shares a lifecycle.

Layout Cost
v0.1: T1 results through Redis ~140 ms per turn
process per interview most of the isolation, without the hop

followUps.html:
Yes.

400 ms blockVAD frames and STT streaming queue upspeech detection and interims fall behindnear the endpoint, the turn commits late

Blocking is never safe because the agent isn't speaking.

followUps.html:
The rules depend on every contributor knowing them.

Enforce mechanically How
known sync clients a lint rule in the agent package
regressions a CI test that runs a call with loop-lag assertions
the rest an alert

"We have async everywhere."

real-time-systems-q49.testing: whether you built a regression harness for something most teams judge by ear, and whether you know its limits.
real-time-systems-q49.trap: quoting WER and stopping. WER doesn't tell you whether the words that matter survived, or whether the conversation worked.
real-time-systems-q49.spoken:
Beat Say
1 · Why voice fails silently "Voice quality fails silently. A mangled term doesn't crash anything; it makes a strong candidate look vague. A mispronounced etcd makes the product sound unserious. Neither shows up in a demo or in logs. They only show up when the same fixed inputs run against every config change and you compare the numbers."
2 · Three suites, three questions "So there are three suites answering three questions. Automated STT and TTS goldens: does the pipeline hear and say the words that matter? Second, 25 manual conversation cases on a live call: barge-in, clarification, probe budget, echo, reconnect. Third, a scoring reference set for whether the scores are right."
3 · The metrics and gates "The goldens are twenty sentences across categories, technical vocabulary, numbers, Indian context, homophone traps, turned into audio with two US voices and an Indian-accent voice. The gates: key-term recall at 90 percent and WER at 15 on the categories we claim; a pronunciation round trip at 85 percent; and TTS first byte at 300 milliseconds warm."
4 · The improvement loop "The loop is one change per run, with the old config beside the new one, read the misses not the averages, pin the version, and every live failure becomes a new golden item."
5 · What's still synthetic "Limits: it is all synthetic, studio-clean speech, which overstates accuracy. Recording real voices on real laptop mics is the most valuable next step."
Close "Fixed inputs, gated on what we claim, and honest about what is synthetic."

stages.name: Why voice fails silently
stages.html:
Error Why nothing alerts
"idempotent" heard as "item potent" a valid English phrase: no error, no log line
a wrong pronunciation sounds fine to anyone who doesn't know the term
  • "idempotent" → "item potent" is a valid English phrase: no error, no alert.
  • A wrong pronunciation sounds fine to anyone who doesn't know the term.
  • Only fixed inputs, run every time, make these visible.

stages.name: Three suites, three questions
stages.html:
Suite Question How
STT/TTS goldens does it hear and say the words that matter? automated, goldens.stt_tts.run
conversation cases does a real call behave? manual, 25 cases on a live call
scoring reference set are the scores right and repeatable? automated scorer goldens (provisional labels)

stages.name: The metrics and gates
stages.html:
Prove it — why key-term recall, not just WER (run with Python 3):

def wer(ref, hyp):
    r, h = ref.split(), hyp.split()
    d = list(range(len(h) + 1))
    for i, rw in enumerate(r, 1):
        prev, d[0] = d[0], i
        for j, hw in enumerate(h, 1):
            prev, d[j] = d[j], min(d[j] + 1, d[j-1] + 1, prev + (rw != hw))
    return d[-1] / len(r)
ref = "we made the consumers idempotent and retried with backoff"
hyp = "we made the consumers item potent and retried with backoff"
print(f"{wer(ref, hyp):.0%}", "term recall:", int("idempotent" in hyp.split()))
# → 22% term recall: 0
Metric Gate Baseline ( 24 Sep 2026)
key-term recall, gated categories ≥ 90% 99%
WER, gated categories ≤ 15% 1.7%
lexicon round trip ≥ 85% 100% (after the etcd fix)
TTS first byte, warm ≤ 300 ms 319 ms

Reported but not gated: out-of-list terms (50%) and code-switching (50%). Gating them would hide what they're there to show.

stages.name: The improvement loop
stages.claim: one change, side by side, pinned
stages.html:
Loop:read the misseschange one parametercompare with the baselinepin the versiona live failure becomes a golden item
  1. Read the misses: "item potent" → add a keyterm; "that CD" → fix a lexicon entry; empty → language mode.
  2. Change one parameter per run; the baseline config stays in the run.
  3. Pin it: lexicon version and keyterm count are stored on each session, so a transcript traces to its config.
  4. If a fix costs another metric, stop and make it a decision (that's how en-IN vs multilingual was decided).
  5. A live failure becomes a golden item.
  6. Suspect the harness first: a benchmark bug once read TTS first byte as 1.3 s.

stages.name: What's still synthetic
stages.claim: and what isn't measured at all
stages.html:
Gap State
human recordings next: the 20 items read by several people on real mics, reported per cohort
noise brown noise and hum down to 5 dB SNR cost only 3–4 points of recall
turn-detection cut-off rate, barge-in false positives manual cases only; not in the automated suites
  • Synthetic audio is a regression baseline; human recordings are the truth. Next: the 20 items read by several people on real mics, reported per cohort.
  • A noise study (brown noise + hum, down to 5 dB SNR) showed noise costs only 3–4 points of recall; the main losses are vocabulary gaps and turn splits.
  • Not in the automated suites yet: turn-detection cut-off rate and barge-in false positives (manual cases only).

followUps.question: Why synthesise test audio at all?
followUps.html:
It is cheap, repeatable and cached.

Synthetic audio is
right for regressions: did this change make it worse?
wrong for absolute accuracy claims

Re-runs only pay for transcription.

followUps.question: "Our WER is 1.7%, so STT is solved."
followUps.html:
On the categories we claim, with synthetic voices.

Slice Number

out-of-list terms 50% recall
real laptop mics and accents worse; not yet measured

A regression baseline, not a production accuracy.

followUps.question: How would you measure the conversation, not the words?
followUps.html:
From per-turn logs and the live call cases.

Source Covers
per-turn metrics end-to-end latency, end-of-turn delay, interruptions and false interruptions, echo suppressions, text-fallback rate
the 25 call cases behaviours: probe budget, clarification, reconnect

See Q19 for the layered view.

followUps.html:
The team that changes the config.

vendor upgrade, keyterm list, lexicon entry or LiveKit versionthe same harness in CIship

real-time-systems-q50.testing: whether you understand indirect bias — a protected attribute reaching the outcome through a proxy — and whether you'd raise it yourself.
real-time-systems-q50.trap: "yes, the scorer only sees text." That's the answer that fails the round.
real-time-systems-q50.spoken:
Beat Say
1 · The decision "No, and I'd raise this before anyone else does. Refusing to pass accent to the scorer is necessary, not sufficient."
2 · The constraint "Accent reaches the score through the transcript. Word error rate isn't uniform across Indian-English accents. A candidate transcribed at 88 percent accuracy isn't a worse candidate, but their answer reads as vaguer to the Assessor, and vagueness is exactly what the Prober probes. So they get probed more, their evidence quotes are messier, and the score drifts, without accent ever being an input. The same happens through the turn detector, which is English-only by LiveKit's statement: cut-offs fall more on speakers it wasn't trained on, and a cut-off answer scores worse."
3 · What we rejected "So blind scoring isn't the whole answer; fairness is a measurement problem."
4 · What it cost "What we do: STT confidence is used only to ask for a repeat and never reaches the scorer; the scoring prompts say the transcript is speech recognition and to ignore accent, grammar and filler; the goldens include an Indian-accent voice and ASR-mangled bias traps; keyterm prompting took the Indian-accent voice's term recall to 96 percent. What we owe: STT confidence and cut-off rates aggregated by cohort and reviewed next to adverse-impact reporting. That is specified and not measured."
5 · What would reopen it "Cohort data would reopen it. Today it is a correctly identified problem with no data behind it, and I wouldn't claim more."
Close "Text-only scoring is necessary; measuring the proxies is what makes it fair."

Rule Says

assessors receive text only
stt_confidence never leaves the STT layer; used only for the repeat path

stages.claim: three paths from accent to score

Self-reported and optional, for audit only.

the live Prober reads the raw transcript

In the live Prober.

88% transcriptreads as vaguegets a probe the other candidate doesn'ta different interview

Engineering owns the measurement; hiring compliance owns the decision.

Owner Owns

whoever owns hiring compliance what disparity is acceptable, and what to do about it

spine: What I'd do next, in order
Why the gaps are where they are
real-time-systems-q51.testing: self-awareness and prioritisation. A candidate who says "nothing major" has either not looked or won't say.
real-time-systems-q51.trap: naming a weakness that's really a humble-brag ("we over-engineered for scale"), or listing ten with no order.
real-time-systems-q51.spoken:
Beat Say
1 · The pattern behind the gaps "The pattern is specific: everything that crosses a boundary is well defined, the token contract, the data messages, the Postgres tables, the latency budget, and several things that are computed aren't. That is what a topology-first design produces: asking where something runs forces schemas; it never forces algorithms."
2 · The three I'd name first "The three I'd name first. One: the latency budget has two unverified legs. TTS first byte is 300 milliseconds on paper and 319 measured on one warm stream; under real concurrency it is unknown, and at 450 the budget fails on arithmetic. And the prototype still has an LLM in the turn. Two: fairness is specified, not measured. Accent reaches scores through transcription quality and turn-detector cut-offs, and nobody has measured the turn model on Indian English. Three: scoring quality isn't proven. Our Scorer's first golden run was consistent but generous: mean error about one point, only 54 percent within a point, against labels that still need human review."
3 · What's built vs designed "I keep built and designed apart when I say this: the session, the tiers and the guards are built; speculation, the queue and the gateway are designed."
4 · What I'd do next, in order "Next, in order: load-test TTS and interviews per pod; human recordings across accents with per-cohort metrics; a human-labelled scoring set; then speculative pre-generation with a defined hit metric. That order is by what could invalidate the design, not by what is most fun to build."
5 · Why the gaps are where they are "And the gaps are where they are because Phase 1 can be built without the algorithms, which makes them easy to defer."
Close "Three named gaps, each with the measurement that would close it."
